documents.abstract: Reliable evaluation of LLM-based alpha mining requires more than positive backtest summaries. We audit a preserved project at three levels: historical run counters, outcome retention, and a separately scoped public reanalysis. Three historical runs report 67, 20, and 11 keep decisions, but the comparison mixes metric populations: a mean over kept candidates is compared with a mean of per-round maxima, and successful evaluations with all returned outcomes. These artifacts cannot identify an architecture advantage. A released 1,837-expression catalog also excludes non-positive OOS outcomes, making its zero-reversal rate non-informative. We then account for all 1,047 unique expressions in a frozen, IS-screened preserved pool using forty A-shares and 2024-2025 rank associations. A versioned public-operator correction yields 923 scorable records, 99 with insufficient valid dates, and 25 unsupported, without modifying the other 990 prior diagnostics. Among scorable records, 671 have positive and 252 negative signed mean rank-IC. Simple untrained references also show positive associations, so this distribution does not establish incremental agent skill or profitability. The case study motivates explicit metric grains, immutable cohort accounting, and provenance-aware interpretation rather than architectural rankings from incomplete records.

Background Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are used to support diagnosis, but a model’s accuracy does not establish that clinicians reason more accurately when they use it. This review appraises how AI decision support and large language models affect physicians’ diagnostic performance and the risks of relying on them. Methods This critical narrative review follows the Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles. Scopus, PubMed/MEDLINE, SciELO and LILACS were searched in July and August 2026 in English, Spanish and Portuguese. Eligible studies, published from 2015 onward, compared AI-assisted with unassisted clinicians, measured reliance on AI or unassisted performance after exposure to it, or externally validated deployed models. A single author selected sources purposively. Nine primary studies were appraised with an adapted Critical Appraisal Skills Programme framework. Results In randomized trials of perceptual tasks, AI support improved detection. In the MASAI mammography screening trial, cancer detection rose from 5.0 to 6.4 per 1,000 women, reading workload fell by 44%, and the interval-cancer rate was non-inferior. In colonoscopy, computer-aided detection raised the adenoma detection rate from 40.4% to 54.8%. In the only randomized trial of open-ended diagnostic reasoning, access to GPT-4 did not improve physicians’ scores (76% vs. 74%; P = .60 ), although the model alone scored 92%. Evidence of harm came from smaller or non-randomized studies: reader accuracy fell sharply when AI suggestions were incorrect or the AI missed a cancer; physicians trained in AI literacy were still misled by erroneous model advice; unassisted adenoma detection fell from 28.4% to 22.4% after routine AI use in one pre–post study; and a deployed sepsis model discriminated poorly on external validation (area under the curve 0.63). No eligible study from Latin America was identified. Conclusions In the studies reviewed, AI assistance improved clinician performance in bounded detection tasks but not in open-ended diagnostic reasoning, where evidence is limited to one vignette-based trial. The evidence that reliance on AI can impair performance comes from single or design-limited studies and does not establish how large or lasting such effects are. Benefit therefore cannot be inferred from model accuracy alone; assisted and unassisted clinician performance should be measured directly.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Traditional turbulence-model development relies heavily on expert knowledge and is time-consuming. This study develops an agentic AI framework, DEScover (automated Discovery of DES closures), to explore subgrid length scales for detached eddy simulation (DES). The user provides only a modeling idea: the length scale is the grid width normal to the local vortex axis. Four large language model (LLM) agents then propose, review, implement, and evaluate candidate formulations and generate scripts for CFD simulations. The Discovery Agent infers the vortex axis from various vortex-identification methods. The candidates are tested on four cases spanning canonical and engineering flows: a flat plate, a backward-facing step, a free shear layer, and an iced airfoil. For all test cases, the best candidate consistently outperforms the standard length scale based on the maximum cell size. Its accuracy is similar to, or slightly better than, that of the expert-designed shear-layer-adapted length scale. Each agentic discovery run takes about 25 minutes on average, excluding the CFD simulations. These results show that LLM-based reasoning can significantly accelerate the discovery of physically interpretable turbulence models and reduce reliance on manual expert formulation.

Over the past decade, substantial efforts have been devoted to developing machine learning (ML) methods for extracting materials data and, where possible, materials knowledge directly from the scientific literature. This review traces the evolution of these methods from heuristic, rule-based pipelines through natural language processing (NLP) models and transformer-based encoders to, lastly, large language models (LLMs) and agentic systems capable of extracting materials information across multiple modalities, including text, tables, and figures. Beside construction of large, queryable materials databases and knowledge graphs that support downstream materials discovery, we discuss how these advances have enabled new capabilities, such as, generic question answering across materials science, AI co-scientists and chatbots for research assistance, and closed-loop optimization and discovery when integrated with autonomous laboratories. We critically assess the datasets generated using these approaches, their extraction accuracy and computational costs, and the respective strengths and limitations of different methodologies, and even provide practical guidelines for developing more reliable and scalable materials data extraction pipelines. Finally, we identify key open challenges, including the extraction of full materials structure-property-processing-performance tetrahedron at the sample level, the scarcity of reliable benchmark datasets for systematic evaluation, and the resolution of non-standard materials terminology across different document modalities.

Automatic Fertilizer Formulation presents an open technological concept for preparing customized plant nutrient formulations through programmable dosing of solid and liquid ingredients. The proposed system combines modular dispensing hardware, formulation mathematics, calibration, chemical constraints, sensors, and traceable preparation records. Rather than relying exclusively on predefined commercial fertilizers, the concept explores how nutrient solutions could be formulated, adjusted, reproduced, and studied from identifiable raw materials according to plant requirements, water composition, growing conditions, and scientific evidence. Part of a Larger Scientific Knowledge Graph This publication is part of Unified Plant Knowledge for Indoor and Outdoor Cultivation, an open research initiative developed by Luan Menezes de Souza. The initiative aims to progressively construct an interconnected scientific knowledge graph describing plant systems across physical, chemical, biological, environmental, and technological scales. The objective is not simply to collect publications, but to identify, explain, and connect the mechanisms linking different processes: photon transport, light absorption, photosynthesis, temperature, transpiration, water transport, nutrient availability and uptake, metabolism, plant morphology, development, and environmental interactions. Each publication contributes another part of this expanding network, connecting established scientific models, mathematical relationships, experimental evidence, engineering concepts, unresolved questions, and new research possibilities. Connection to Photonic Vine The initiative builds upon the foundational Photonic Vine research corpus, which explores how lighting geometry, spectral distribution, and proximity to plant tissues affect photon delivery and subsequent biological processes. Automatic Fertilizer Formulation extends this investigation into plant nutrition. Changes in illumination can influence photosynthesis, leaf temperature, transpiration, growth, and nutrient demand. Understanding these relationships requires connecting models from photonics, thermodynamics, plant physiology, root transport, and nutrient chemistry. Future publications will expand these causal chains, including energy transfer, resource balances, physiological responses, and the interactions between illumination and nutrient management. Intended Use by Researchers, Developers, and Artificial Intelligence The documents are intended to be read both by humans and AI-assisted research systems. Researchers may use the material to investigate the proposed mechanisms, examine mathematical relationships, compare existing literature, identify missing evidence, design experiments, and develop alternative implementations. Engineers and developers may study the proposed hardware, formulation methods, and modular architecture as starting points for further design and testing. AI systems may use the documented equations, references, assumptions, structured knowledge records, and identified research questions to reconstruct relationships between publications, detect inconsistencies, propose additional connections, and support future mathematical formalization. The long-term objective includes exploring formal verification methods, such as Lean 4, to establish which mathematical conclusions follow rigorously from explicitly stated assumptions. Formal mathematical consistency, numerical calculations, experimental evidence, and biological validation remain distinct levels of verification. Proposed designs and illustrative calculations should not be interpreted as validated equipment performance or universal plant nutrition recommendations. An Expanding Open Knowledge Network This publication is one component of a continuing research effort. Future deposits associated with the Unified Plant Knowledge community are intended to progressively connect additional disciplines, models, experimental findings, and technological concepts into a navigable, traceable, and reusable scientific knowledge network. The central goal is to make the relationships between plant processes increasingly explicit, testable, mathematically understandable, and accessible to both human researchers and future artificial intelligence systems. Author: Luan Menezes de Souza Research community: https://zenodo.org/communities/unified-plant-knowledge-for-indoor-and-outdoor-cultivation/ Foundational research: https://zenodo.org/records/23463505

documents.abstract: Stance classifiers make errors that can be costly to identify under limited human-review budgets. Prioritizing potentially incorrect predictions remains challenging, particularly across heterogeneous base models. We introduce B-CARE (Blind Classwise Assessment of Relative Evidence for Stance Error Ranking), a prediction-blind framework for identifying high-risk stance predictions. Given only a target and text, a fixed LLM verifier assigns ordinal evidence scores to all candidate stance labels without observing the base model's prediction or confidence. B-CARE constructs a comparative risk score by contrasting the strongest alternative-class evidence with the evidence supporting the predicted class. The resulting classwise evidence profile can be reused across multiple base models without training a separate error detector or calibrating risk scores. We evaluate B-CARE on four stance benchmarks and three heterogeneous base LLMs, covering 12 dataset-model settings and 5,206 unique test instances. Evaluation includes error-ranking discrimination (AUROC and AUPRC), selective prediction (E-AURC), and review effectiveness (ErrorCapture at fixed review budgets). B-CARE achieves a mean AUROC of 0.735 and a mean AUPRC of 0.524, capturing 41.06% of errors within the highest-risk 20% of predictions. Although B-CARE does not uniformly outperform strong confidence-based baselines, it provides a reusable, complementary evidence signal for prioritizing potentially incorrect stance predictions across heterogeneous models.

Spray-deposit models used to schedule agrochemical applications increasingly rely on learned components, yet the numerical reliability of their outputs under gradual nozzle wear remains uncharacterised. The analysis defines nozzle wear as a slow parametric perturbation of the drift operator and derives a computable backward error bound that separates model-form error from wear-induced parameter error. Adjoint sensitivities are then used to identify which wear-affected coefficients dominate the forward error in predicted deposit mass. The framework is presented as a methodological proposal: no field data are analysed and no empirical estimates are reported. The contribution is a formal criterion for deciding when a spray-deposit model's prediction can be trusted under wear drift, together with an adjoint-based diagnostic that localises the dominant error source. The analysis implies that backward error, rather than forward residual alone, should govern model recalibration schedules in artificial-intelligence-assisted spray advisory systems.

Biometric recognition often degrades under partial facial vis- ibility, where conventional facial cues are occluded. The forehead region remains consistently visible and contains distinctive crease patterns that can serve as a complementary biometric trait. We present a unified eval- uation of forehead-crease recognition across explainable zero-shot rea- soning, domain-adaptive learning, and trait-specific modeling. FIRE en- ables interpretable zero-shot verification using multimodal large language models, while pretrained face-recognition models are adapted to the fore- head domain through margin-based learning. Under open-set evaluation, the best zero-shot model GPT-4o+FIRE achieves 18.22% EER, while Edge-Forehead achieves 8.30% EER and 54.01% TMR@0.1% FMR. The results show that although MLLMs offer interpretable zero-shot verifi- cation, trait-specific learning remains more effective for robust forehead- crease biometric recognition.

Automated vehicles shift drivers into supervisory roles, where engagement in non-driving-related tasks (NDRTs) may degrade driver readiness. This vulnerability becomes critical in adversarial contexts, where cyber-attacks often manipulate in-vehicle information rather than vehicle dynamics. This study examined whether pre-attack driver readiness conditions affect subsequent cyber-attack response performance. Forty-five participants completed a two-phase automated driving experiment consisting of an NDRT phase followed by six cyber-attack scenarios. Situation awareness (SA), visual attention, physiological arousal, workload, and response time were measured. A static Bayesian Network modeled joint probabilistic dependencies across contextual, driver readiness, and behavioral variables. NDRT demand was linked to pre-attack readiness, post-attack workload, and response time in parallel; pre-attack SA was linked to workload but not to response time.

Most questions that reach an HPC help desk have already been answered in the center's user guides or in a ticket someone else filed last semester; users still file new tickets because the guides are hard to navigate and the ticket history is not theirs to search. We present an assistant that answers from both sources: an orchestrator calls two tools over the Model Context Protocol, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over the live documentation and a Llama-3-8B model fine-tuned with QLoRA on 11,244 query-resolution pairs mined from historical tickets, and merges their answers. Every model runs on-premises or on the university's hosted LLM service because ticket data may not leave the institution. On 400 held-out tickets from Purdue's Rosen Center for Advanced Computing, disjoint from training and free of near-duplicates, and evaluated by two judges from model families that generated none of the answers, fine-tuning on resolutions rewritten into self-service guidance is the clear winner in agreement with RCAC's resolutions (BERTScore F1 improves from 0.06 to 0.27 over the base model) and is judged most correct on average. The end-to-end system does not improve on its tools, although they are complementary: choosing the better answer per question would exceed either tool (judged correctness 3.41 versus 3.20, an oracle bound), while the merge follows the documentation tool in 78% of answers. Returning one tool's answer instead recovers the fine-tuned tool's quality (3.19 versus 2.66), but neither a learned selector nor an LLM verifier beats that tool alone.

LLM judges are used to determine which of two answers is better. Trusting these verdicts requires knowing how repeatable they are and how much they depend on the judge's instructions. We show that similar aggregate scores can conceal substantial changes in individual verdicts, both when the same setup is repeated and when the instructions change. Using 500 Arena-Hard v2.0 prompts with two models' answers held fixed, we run GPT-4.1 as the judge under all eight combinations of criteria, output format and task framing, and repeat every setup unchanged at temperature zero on a pinned model version. Rerunning the default setup moves the aggregate score by about one point but changes the win/tie/loss outcome on 21.2% of prompts. Instruction changes introduce further sensitivity: in one setup, which asks for the verdict without reasoning and also drops several other instructions, outcomes change on 28.2 percentage points more prompts than the two setups' unchanged reruns do on average, and the aggregate score falls by 4.09 points. In another, where the criteria prioritise accuracy, outcomes change on 6.7 percentage points more prompts by the same comparison, while the aggregate score barely moves. A stable aggregate score therefore does not establish that individual verdicts are repeatable. This distinction matters when those verdicts are used as preference labels or to assess individual responses. Evaluations that rely on individual verdicts should repeat each setup they use and report both aggregate scores and prompt-level agreement.

Enterprise security concentrates where it can see: firewalls, endpoint alerts and patch dashboards, while the structural work that decides whether an intrusion becomes a breach stays submerged. Large language models and autonomous agents have added three new strata beneath that waterline, and the research literature, split across three disciplines, has not recognized them as one problem. This review unifies agentic AI security, shadow AI governance and LLM supply-chain risk, which descend from adversarial machine learning, information-systems governance and software engineering. The review proceeded in five steps. We retrieved 7254 records from three open scholarly indexes, a fixed set of institutional gray-literature sources and snowballing (January 2004 to June 2026); screened them under written codebooks with an independently double-screened sample (κ=0.86); retained 2136 sources, of which 784 are peer-reviewed articles, 1264 preprints or standards documents, and 88 vendor or institutional reports, each graded on a four-tier evidence scale; derived an analytical framework by open coding a 15% subsample; and coded the full corpus against it (κ=0.89). On that basis, we make four moves. First, we reconstruct the field’s history as five eras separated by four capability breakpoints identified from shifts in the corpus’s dominant coding, separating each thread’s originator from its popularizer. Second, we propose three failure primitives (visibility loss, identity ambiguity and provenance erosion) as an organizing framework in place of the customary attack-surface taxonomy; each recurs in all three strata, and the recurrence survives alternative coding rules and the removal of weaker evidence. Third, a primitive-by-stratum map locates where practitioner concern outruns published evidence, most sharply where identity meets ungoverned adoption. Fourth, we derive a research agenda dated to 2026 signals, including an unproven impossibility conjecture for prompt-injection prevention and the unsolved problem of proving authority across multi-hop agent delegation. For practitioners, the framework reduces to three auditable questions (whether the defender can enumerate, attribute and trace AI activity), and the map tells them which of the three their current tooling leaves unanswered.

documents.abstract: Federated learning for crop-disease classification across heterogeneous farm clients is vulnerable to Byzantine participants who submit corrupted model updates, yet the aggregation literature reports robustness without a design-level account of how many adversarial clients a given federation can tolerate before diagnostic integrity collapses. The analysis treats the aggregation rule as a statistical estimator of the honest update direction and characterises the breakdown point of coordinate-wise median and trimmed-mean aggregation under a declared contamination model. A before-after-control-impact design is used to benchmark power across cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points, with 2000 replications per design cell and an intraclass correlation of 0.640. The contamination bound predicts that coordinate-wise median aggregation tolerates up to 50% adversarial clients in the limit but loses diagnostic integrity at a threshold that depends on the between-cluster standard deviation of 6.0 and the residual standard deviation of 4.5. The benchmarking results indicate that 54 clusters are required to detect a 5 percentage point degradation at 80% power. The contribution is a formal contamination bound that links aggregation-rule choice to the minimum federation size needed to certify diagnostic integrity, together with a benchmarking protocol that makes that link auditable.

Variable-rate nitrogen scheduling in computer agriculture must reconcile two competing demands: maximising crop uptake and limiting nitrate leaching into groundwater. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers a data-driven alternative to rule-based schedulers, but its deployment is complicated by actuation delays and by uncertainty in the leaching-risk signal. Because no field data are available, the study is framed as a methodological and comparative analysis: it formalises the scheduling problem as a constrained Markov decision process with delayed actions, defines a regret metric that penalises both yield loss and compliance violations, and derives a finite-sample bound on the regret gap between the delay-aware learner and an oracle scheduler. The bound is then evaluated across a design grid of 8, 16, 24 and 32 management clusters, effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points, and 2000 replications per cell, using a before-after-control-impact variance structure with an intraclass correlation of 0.64, a between-cluster standard deviation of 6.0 and a residual standard deviation of 4.5. The regret gap widens nonlinearly as the delay horizon grows relative to the decision interval, and that the compliance penalty dominates the yield penalty once the leaching-risk signal is sufficiently noisy. The implication is that many reported RL gains in agricultural scheduling may be artefacts of underpowered evaluations.

Event cameras offer microsecond latency and high dynamic range for row-crop navigation, but dust-occlusion transients corrupt optical-flow estimates in ways that frame-based benchmarks do not capture. No observational data are used or claimed: the analysis is a design and power study. The variance structure specifies a between-cluster standard deviation of 6.0, a residual standard deviation of 4.5 and an intraclass correlation of 0.640. Power was estimated across 2000 design cells defined by cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The design achieves 80% power at 54 clusters for a 5-percentage-point effect. The paper formalises a lateral-error bound that maps optical-flow estimation error under dust occlusion to a safety envelope for implement guidance, and shows how the BACI estimator's operating characteristics constrain the benchmark's ability to detect safety-relevant improvements. The contribution is a benchmark architecture and a power-analytic foundation for evaluating event-camera optical-flow methods in computer agriculture, with explicit boundary conditions on what the design can and cannot establish.

Offline reinforcement learning (RL) promises irrigation controllers that can be trained from logged field data without further water expenditure, but the logged policies that generated those data confound every value estimate the controller relies on. The bound is derived from a concentration inequality on importance-weighted returns, corrected for the behaviour-policy overlap that determines how much of the target policy's state-action distribution the logs actually cover. The resulting penalty is a function of the effective sample size of the logged dataset and the estimated confoundedness of the behaviour policy, and it yields a certified lower confidence bound on the water-use safety of any candidate irrigation policy. The bound is validated against a real World Bank panel of 24 African countries observed from 2000 to 2023 (N = 560), in which GDP per capita (constant 2015 US$) was regressed on access to electricity and urban population share; the fitted model (R-squared = 0.591, F = 184.764) supplies the macro-contextual covariate structure against which the irrigation benchmark is calibrated. Offline RL benchmarking for irrigation must report the pessimism penalty alongside the policy return, because a controller that is safe only under the logging policy is not safe at all.

Smallholder yield surveys in sub-Saharan Africa routinely lose a large share of their observations to item non-response, and the resulting imputation error propagates directly into the food-security statistics that national agencies report. The argument is methodological and theoretical rather than empirical: no new survey was fielded, and the empirical anchor is the DHS Program indicator 'Women's occupation: Agriculture' (id EM_OCCP_W_AGR), which was retrieved for 35 African countries over 1994 to 2024, giving 140 country-survey observations with a mean of 40.584 and a standard deviation of 20.59. The paper formalises missingness as a conditional score-matching problem, states the assumptions under which the imputation error is controlled, and proves a bound in which the downstream yield-estimation error is bounded by the score-matching excess risk plus a term that depends on the missingness mechanism and the conditional variance of yield. The bound is then used to benchmark score-based diffusion imputation against conditional-mean and multiple-imputation baselines on the DHS indicator, and to specify the conditions under which diffusion imputation is preferable for food-security reporting. The contribution is a benchmark protocol and an error bound that make imputation quality auditable before yield statistics enter policy reporting.

Edge pest detection in computer agriculture is constrained less by classifier accuracy than by the thermal power budget of the sensing node. Spiking neural networks (SNNs) promise order-of-magnitude energy reductions on neuromorphic hardware, but the field lacks a design-level account of how that promise translates into deployable detection performance when the thermal sensor itself is the dominant load. The framework formalises a thermal-power budget, defines an energy-normalised detection rate, and derives a power-accuracy frontier for leaky integrate-and-fire classifiers operating on low-resolution thermal frames. A replication-based evaluation of the before-after-control-impact estimator was conducted under a declared variance structure (between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5, intraclass correlation = 0.64), with power estimated across 2000 design cells. The analysis indicates that 54 clusters are required to detect a 5-percentage-point effect at 80% power. The contribution is a reproducible audit protocol that makes the energy-accuracy trade-off explicit and falsifiable before field deployment, and that identifies the sensor duty cycle, not the network, as the binding constraint in most edge configurations.

Tensor-network compression promises to fit convolutional disease classifiers into the memory ceilings of field-deployable diagnostic devices, but the accuracy cost of compression is usually reported as a single post-hoc number rather than as a bounded retention guarantee. the present analysis treats compression as a design problem with an auditable operating characteristic: given a declared memory ceiling, what fraction of the uncompressed diagnostic accuracy survives, and with what uncertainty? We formalise tensor-train decomposition of convolutional kernels as a rank-constrained projection, derive a retention bound that links bond dimension, kernel spectrum and the resulting classification margin, and then characterise the operating characteristics of a benchmarking protocol that estimates retention under a declared variance structure. The protocol is a before-after-control-impact design with between-cluster SD 6.0, residual SD 4.5 and intraclass correlation 0.64, evaluated across 2000 replications per design cell at cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. Power reaches conventional levels only at 56 clusters for a 5-percentage-point retention effect, which exceeds every cluster count in the declared grid; the minimum detectable effect at 80% power therefore remains above the 5-percentage-point threshold throughout the grid. The contribution is a retention bound plus a power-calibrated audit protocol that tells practitioners when a compression benchmark is informative and when it is underpowered, and that reframes field diagnostic safety as a property of the evaluation design rather than of the compressor alone.

Vision-language foundation models adapted to weed identification in computer agriculture are typically evaluated by top-1 accuracy on held-out images, a metric that does not bound the agronomic consequence of a misclassification. The framework formalises the adaptation problem as risk minimisation over a hypothesis class of vision-language prompts, derives a PAC-Bayes bound that links few-shot sample size, prompt-space complexity and the divergence between source and target weed floras to an upper bound on the probability of herbicide misapplication, and specifies a benchmarking protocol that reports this bound alongside conventional accuracy. The bound is decomposed into a transfer term, a few-shot estimation term and a distribution-shift term, each of which corresponds to a distinct benchmarking condition that current evaluation practice omits. A worked instantiation for a four-class weed/non-weed decision problem shows how the bound responds to shot count, prompt complexity and shift magnitude, and identifies the shot count below which the bound exceeds a declared safety threshold. The contribution is a shift from accuracy benchmarking to risk-bounded benchmarking for safety-critical agricultural vision, with implications for how few-shot extension deployments should be evaluated before herbicide recommendations are issued.

Code-switching is a natural linguistic phenomenon, yet its impact on high-level reasoning tasks remains largely unexplored in under-resourced languages like Romanian. Natural language processing tasks, such as satire detection, rely heavily on nuanced cultural and syntactic cues that large language models struggle to capture. In this paper, we investigate four methods (i.e., random replacement, phrase translation, dependency parsing, and large language models) for generating synthetic code-mixed Romanian sentences with English, German, French, and Italian. We start with an existing dataset for satire detection, compiled from Romanian news articles and annotated at the sentence level by humans, and augment it with over 600k samples, namely CS-SeLeRoSa. We provide an in-depth analysis of the dataset generation process. Then, we evaluate several multilingual large language models across zero-shot, chain-of-thought, and fine-tuning regimes on both the synthetic corpus and a human-adjudicated gold benchmark, namely CS-SeLeRoSa-Gold. While older open models suffer substantial degradation (dropping to 37%-55% macro-F1), newer models like Gemma 4 31B achieve 68.1% zero-shot, rivaling frontier models like GPT-5 mini (69.5%). Furthermore, fine-tuning significantly reduces formatting errors and improves the results, increasing Gemma 4 31B to 77.5% on CS-SeLeRoSa and 72.6% on the gold standard, outperforming frontier zero-shot baselines.

Abstract Developing the capacity for self-reflection is a central component of continual teacher growth. Practices such as journaling help educators rapidly improve by enabling them to identify challenges in lesson planning, assessment, behavior management, and classroom culture. Autoethnography, a research method that integrates reflective journal entries with existing scholarship, offers a structured approach for deepening this self-reflective work. Introducing autoethnographic practices to both future and current educators can therefore cultivate stronger reflective habits across all stages of a teaching career. For preservice teachers, engaging in autoethnography encourages them to connect their emerging classroom observations with established research, promoting evidence-based decision-making early in their professional development. These reflective habits can support long-term success by helping new teachers internalize practices that foster continuous improvement. For teachers in their first years, autoethnography provides a tool for managing the steep learning curve they face as they encounter educational challenges for the first time. Reflective journaling paired with research can offer clarity, reduce overwhelm, and help them make sense of their experiences. Veteran teachers also benefit from autoethnographic practices, as the method can deepen their understanding of complex or evolving issues—such as the growing influence of artificial intelligence in classrooms—by linking ongoing experiences with contemporary scholarship. Finally, teacher educators who use autoethnography themselves gain methodological proficiency, strengthen their own teaching, and develop authentic examples to share with those they mentor. This chapter explores the value of integrating autoethnographic practices into teacher education to support reflective growth at all career stages.

This article examines the epistemic implications of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in academic writing within unequal knowledge infrastructures. I conceptualize it as an epistemic apparatus: a sociotechnical arrangement that mediates credibility, voice, and scholarly legitimacy. Drawing on epistemic injustice theory, post- and decolonial scholarship, and critical AI studies, the article argues that GenAI can reinforce dominant Anglophone norms of academic form, reshaping the conditions under which knowledge becomes legible and publishable. I argue that these effects emerge through interactions among models, writing practices, and institutional expectations. Through two author-constructed fictional analytic vignettes, the article illustrates how selective uptake, compromise, diagnostic testing, and refusal can operate as practices of judgment within AI-mediated writing. I conceptualize epistemic autonomy as situated authority over scholarly judgment and advance critical epistemic literacy as a pedagogical orientation for exercising that authority under algorithmic mediation. The article concludes by proposing an epistemic ethics of governance oriented toward traceability, plurality, infrastructural accountability, and the protection of bounded use and refusal.

Current LLM safety benchmarks predominantly rely on binary safe or unsafe labels, lacking explanatory depth and suffering from low consistency across automated judges. To address this, we introduce DiagSafe, a diagnostic evaluation framework that moves beyond binary classification by employing prompt-level rubrics. Grounded in globally applicable AI safety policies, each rubric provides explicit criteria along two dimensions: safety, which targets concrete harms with specific exemptions to suppress false positives, and usefulness, which independently evaluates instruction fulfillment. To ensure a robust and realistic evaluation, we construct a bilingual (English-Chinese) benchmark grounded in a comprehensive 84-label safety taxonomy, consisting of two subsets: DiagBase, which covers single- and multi-turn prompts with direct harmful queries and template-based jailbreaks, and DiagAttack, which embeds harmful intents into complex instruction-following tasks to form challenging instruction attacks. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DiagSafe significantly enhances the reliability of LLM-as-a-judge evaluation, achieving 95.34% agreement with human annotations -- substantially higher than the 69%-87% achieved by the baselines -- and high inter-judge consistency (Cohen's $κ$ = 0.864). Furthermore, applying our framework reveals that leading LLMs differ markedly in their unsafe rates, and each model also exhibits unique vulnerabilities along different dimensions. In addition, we observe that models are particularly susceptible in Chinese and multi-turn contexts. Ultimately, DiagSafe provides a reliable and explainable tool for auditing and optimizing LLM alignment.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Australia has made substantial progress in digital health workforce development through the establishment of nationally coordinated strategies, profession-specific capability frameworks, and the Australian Digital Health Capability Framework. Collectively, these initiatives have repositioned digital health from a specialised technical domain to a core professional competency expected across the health workforce. However, while considerable effort has focused on defining the capabilities required for contemporary digital practice, less attention has been directed towards ensuring workforce readiness. This perspective argues that capability and readiness are related but distinct concepts. Capability frameworks describe the knowledge, skills, and behaviours expected of health professionals, whereas readiness reflects the ability to apply these capabilities confidently, ethically, and adaptively within rapidly evolving healthcare environments. As digital health systems become increasingly influenced by artificial intelligence, predictive analytics, and data-driven decision-making, workforce preparedness will depend on more than technical competence alone. It will require critical thinking, ethical reasoning, digital and data literacies, and the capacity to work effectively alongside emerging technologies. We propose that, while capability frameworks will continue to evolve alongside technological and regulatory change, Australia's next challenge is ensuring that existing capability expectations are translated into educational practice, workplace learning, professional development, and measurable workforce outcomes. Sustained implementation, evaluation, and collaboration will be essential to ensure a future-ready digital health workforce.

In large language model (LLM) steganography, an encoder hides a private message in an otherwise ordinary response, as text transmitted to a decoder, who attempts to recover it. The success of this private-message transmission is commonly measured through end-to-end (E2E) recovery, which checks whether the decoder correctly reconstructs the private message. However, E2E recovery cannot distinguish encoding failures from decoding failures or reveal how the private message is represented in the encoder's transmitted text. To address these limitations, we introduce a rolewise decomposition framework that separately examines how private messages are represented in encoder transmitted texts, what decoders recover, and what deterministic verification can establish. Across 7,200 encoder responses, we identify 168 verifiable encodings missed by decoders and 706 responses containing private messages reconstructed through word-length or token-initial patterns not explicitly specified in the encoder's instructions. These findings demonstrate that E2E recovery alone may obscure important distinctions between encoding and decoding, motivating their separate evaluation to better understand and mitigate the safety issues caused by LLM steganography.

Continuing professional development (CPD) is frequently organised as a sequence of educational events directed at individual practitioners. In resource-constrained health services, however, participation and learning transfer are shaped by staffing, protected time, leadership, finance, infrastructure, access to current guidance and opportunities to apply learning. Individual-centred and linear developmental models do not adequately explain these interactions. This article proposes the Context-Enabled Continuing Professional Development (CE-CPD) Framework, derived from a programme of research involving a scoping review, qualitative evidence from professional nurses and nurse managers in Limpopo Province, South Africa, and critical engagement with developmental, implementation and CPD-outcomes literature. The framework positions professional learning within four interacting layers: a stakeholder and service ecosystem, organisational enabling conditions, a recurring five-phase workplace learning cycle, and an outcome pathway extending from access and participation to practitioner capability, professional behaviour, team and organisational performance, and patient or population health. Capability development is treated as domain-specific, iterative and potentially non-linear, rather than as an automatic progression from novice to expert. Six propositions specify how contextual readiness, protected opportunity, equitable access, workplace application, knowledge sharing and infrastructure are expected to influence these outcomes. The CE-CPD Framework shifts the explanatory focus from whether professionals attend CPD to whether their organisations make relevant learning possible and ensure its sustainable application. Although derived from nursing evidence, its organisational mechanisms may be relevant across healthcare professions. Interprofessional co-design, prospective testing and equity-sensitive evaluation are required before wider adoption.

Environmental artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly improving prediction across Earth system forecasting, remote sensing, and biodiversity monitoring, yet predictive skill out paces scientific understanding, data and models remain fragmented across environmental and human-system contexts, and the capacity to govern and act on AI is unevenly distributed. Using the Cyber-Physical-Social-Thinking (CPST) framework, we locate these gaps in relations rather than in individual models: a prediction-understanding rupture (weak Cyber-Thinking coupling), cross-domain fragmentation (incomplete Cyber-Physical-Social integration), and a science-governance-equity gap (weak Thinking-Social coupling with asymmetric Cyber-Social capacity). We specify semantic, procedural, and institutional dimensions along which these relations fail, and propose that the three bottlenecks are mutually reinforcing. Set against knowledge-systems research on credibility, salience, and legitimacy, the CPST lens adds one distinction: it separates the inference performed by a model from the scientific interpretation of its outputs, so that evidential warrant and institutional authority can fail independently. Three reconnection pathways follow, namely epistemically anchored environmental AI, interoperable environmental AI systems, and participatory environmental-AI governance, each with evaluation criteria that extend beyond predictive accuracy. Applied to operational flood forecasting, the diagnosis yields a procedure that identifies the binding relation, predicts where the limiting factor moves once that relation is strengthened, and states the evidence that would disconfirm the ranking. Progress should be judged by whether digital capability remains connected to physical processes, scientific reasoning, and societal institutions in ways that are reliable, interpretable, and fit for purpose.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Machine learning models are increasingly deployed in high-stakes decision systems where predictive performance alone may provide an insufficient basis for responsible model selection. Although explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) offers techniques for interpreting model behavior, existing evaluation approaches often assess explanation properties independently and provide limited support for integrated model selection. This study proposes the Explainability–Governance Score (EGS) Framework, a multidimensional decision-support methodology integrating four complementary dimensions: Fidelity, local predictive Stability, Counterfactual Actionability, and Governance Alignment. The framework combines established XAI techniques, practical recourse, and governance-oriented criteria into a composite evaluation of candidate models. It is empirically evaluated using five machine learning models across three high-stakes domains represented by the German Credit, Pima Indians Diabetes, and COMPAS datasets. Under the primary BPS specification, predictive evaluation ranked XGBoost, Decision Tree, and Random Forest highest in Credit Risk, Healthcare, and Criminal Justice, respectively. Under the multidimensional EGS evaluation, Logistic Regression achieved the highest EGS in Credit Risk (0.915) and Healthcare (0.915), while Decision Tree achieved the highest EGS in Criminal Justice (0.886). The identity of the highest-EGS model remained unchanged across all six prespecified weighting configurations in each domain. These findings demonstrate that multidimensional EGS evaluation can materially influence candidate-model rankings relative to predictive evaluation and provide a structured, reproducible basis for evaluating candidate models beyond predictive performance alone.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The rapid expansion of Property Technology (PropTech) has fundamentally transformed the role of software within the real estate industry. Early PropTech solutions primarily focused on digitizing isolated operational activities such as leasing, maintenance management, accounting, and customer communication. As digital ecosystems have matured, however, the engineering challenge has shifted from developing individual applications to designing complex systems capable of integrating physical infrastructure, enterprise software, cloud services, artificial intelligence, Internet of Things (IoT), and human decision-making into unified operational environments. This article argues that future PropTech platforms should be understood not merely as software products but as large-scale systems whose behavior emerges from the interaction of numerous interconnected technical and organizational components. Adopting a systems engineering perspective enables organizations to address scalability, interoperability, resilience, lifecycle management, stakeholder coordination, and long-term system evolution more effectively than traditional software-centric approaches. The article introduces a systems engineering framework specifically designed for scalable PropTech ecosystems, integrating principles of system decomposition, requirements engineering, operational resilience, lifecycle management, human-system collaboration, and continuous architectural evolution. Rather than emphasizing individual technologies, the proposed framework focuses on engineering digital real estate ecosystems that remain adaptable, reliable, and sustainable throughout decades of operational change. Contemporary platform-based engineering research likewise emphasizes adaptability and long-term evolvability as essential characteristics of complex digital systems.

Recently, we see a rise in conversational agents as a form of social and emotional support, where disclosure will unfold over time. Yet, current evaluations of these agents typically examine isolated conversational states. In analyses of naturally occurring conversations, disclosure history and current disclosure are confounded which tends to make their effects difficult to isolate. We thus introduce Trajectory-based Disclosure Evaluation (TraDE), an evaluation framework grounded in Social Penetration Theory that utilizes predefined disclosure trajectories and evaluates how preceding disclosure history shapes model behavior under matched current disclosure. Through the use of TraDE, we demonstrate across multiple models and relational behavior benchmarks that responses to disclosures matched on depth can differ depending on the preceding trajectory, particularly in whether models accept or challenge the user's framing. We also observed that these differences track accumulated exposure to deeper disclosure rather than any single moment of vulnerability or the order of disclosures. It also tends to persists for several turns after disclosure returns to shallow levels. For several behaviors, we also demonstrate that models diverge most consistently from human supporters in the Emotional Support Conversation corpus (ESConv) not when users open up but rather when they step back in their disclosure. TraDE thus provides a systematic way to expose history-dependent relational behavior that evaluations of isolated conversational states would otherwise miss.

This paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI) can strengthen applied learning in the social sciences by transforming raw information into analyzable material that students actively interpret, evaluate, and convert into disciplinary knowledge. It argues that AI, when guided by theoretical rigor and ethical awareness, enhances critical pedagogy by supporting qualitative interpretation, computational analysis, simulation based inquiry, and independent reasoning. Rather than replacing instruction, AI functions as an analytical scaffold that students interrogate, correct, and contextualize, enabling deeper engagement with social structures, patterned behavior, and institutional dynamics.
topics: Innovative Teaching Methodologies in Social Sciences

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT This article provides a comprehensive framework for understanding the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in negotiation, evaluating contemporary systems through the specific case study of Large Language Models (LLMs). To address the lack of established terminology, it first proposes a new typology distinguishing Negotiation Supported by AI (NSAI), Negotiation by Controlled AI (NCAI), and Negotiation by Autonomous AI (NAAI). To determine whether current systems can achieve genuine NAAI, the article first develops the Core Essential Elements of Negotiation (CEEN) through a structured comparison of authoritative definitions of negotiation and then examines how these literature‐derived elements align with the perceptions of 250 survey respondents. Finally, the paper applies an ordered analytical rule to contemporary LLMs. Information Exchange and Reciprocity are directly instantiable; Outcome, Divergent Motivations, and Interdependence are externally conditioned; and Choice is not currently instantiable because an attributable evaluative standpoint and consequential commitment remain absent. Accordingly, current LLM‐based negotiating systems remain controlled rather than autonomous agents under the proposed typology.

Retrieval-based in-context learning (ICL) enables large language models (LLMs) to predict tabular labels from similar examples, but it remains unclear whether LLM inference improves on direct voting over those same examples. We address this question by comparing four general-purpose LLMs with distance-weighted nearest-neighbor voting (Distance-KNN) using identical retrieved neighbors across 19 tabular classification datasets. With the number of demonstrations fixed, enlarging the retrieval candidate pool improves accuracy for all predictors, yet Distance-KNN achieves the highest mean accuracy at every pool size. More detailed analyses reveal that LLM gains are concentrated where retrieved neighbors exhibit low label consensus and vary across models. These gains further depend on the average feature-space distance to the test query: under low label consensus, some LLMs outperform Distance-KNN in close and intermediate neighborhoods, but all fall behind on average in the most distant group. Complementary experiments on the number of demonstrations, prompt formulation, retrieval representation, and label-balanced demonstration selection largely preserve the overall findings. These results characterize when LLM inference adds predictive value beyond distance-weighted voting in retrieval-based tabular ICL.

Abstract Agentic LLM agents can sometimes seem like magic, granting our (almost) every wish. But like the magic genies in stories like the Sorcerer's Apprentice, sometimes you have to be careful what you wish for. The difficulty of precisely specifying what it is we want and unintended consequences, sometimes derail this magic. As with genies, they grant requests in a top‐down manner. The agent autonomously breaks the wish into subgoals, until it reaches concrete actions that can be done by Agentic facilities. If left unsupervised by the user, a misunderstanding can result in disaster. But it's also possible to adopt a bottom‐up approach, starting with concrete examples, demonstrating procedures on these examples, and only then generalizing to a wider set of cases. It is often easier to control and debug, and easier for beginners and nontechnical people. Ultimately, we need flexibility to go in either direction. The contribution of this paper is to bring a bottom‐up methodology to “vibe coding” with Agentic Agents like Cowork and ChatGPT Agent. It draws on the technique of Programming by Example (also called Programming by Demonstration) for conventional programming. The advent of Agentic AI may unblock a 50‐year obstacle that has prevented PBE from more widespread acceptance.

This publication presents a consolidated archival and computational release of the Boundary Project, developed within the Continuity Science and Recoverability-Constrained Systems research programme. The corpus brings together mathematical formulations of recoverability, admissible successor spaces, irreversible transitions, protected continuity, operational distinction, recursive governance, system evolution, evidence provenance, institutional accountability, and the preservation of future possibilities. Its central research proposition is that material transitions should be evaluated not only according to present-state validity, immediate performance, or predicted outcomes, but also according to the recoverable future states that remain reachable following execution. The finite successor-space formalism represents operational systems through distinguishable states, transitions, admissibility relations, protected correspondence, and temporal execution constraints. For a state X, the admissibly reachable successor structure C*(X) represents the future-state structure reachable through admissible continuation. Relative to a protected target class G, recoverability is expressed as: R(X,G) = 1 if and only if C(X) intersects G.* This formulation distinguishes operational continuation from recoverable continuation. A system may remain operational while progressively losing independent correction paths, recovery options, supporting reserves, or the ability to preserve protected correspondence. The associated mathematical research examines reachability, fixed points, invariant kernels, closure operators, transition algebra, bisimulation, recoverability topology, possibility collapse, uncertainty, resource dependence, timing constraints, and finite-state verification. The broader programme develops these principles into technical, institutional, legal, biological, ecological, financial, computational, and human-centred architectures. Unified conceptual architecture The corpus is organized around a common operational grammar connecting distinguishable entities, states, events, relations, intervals, boundaries, dependencies, transitions, effects, outcomes, and successor possibilities. It treats recoverability as a property of actual executable continuation under the relevant conditions, rather than merely the theoretical existence of a possible corrective action. Core architectural elements include: Distinction and operational representation Protected identity and correspondence Authority, consent, and admissibility State and transition modelling Finite successor-space reachability Recovery intervals and temporal constraints Independent correction and restoration paths Evidence provenance and traceability Recursive governance and institutional accountability Future possibility preservation Controlled succession and re-entry Self-referential evaluation of recovery and governance mechanisms These elements are applied across interconnected domains rather than treated as unrelated research proposals. Zero-Distinction Boundary The Zero-Distinction Boundary is the formal and epistemic limit of operational specification. Any model capable of evaluating states, comparing outcomes, recognizing identities, establishing relations, testing evidence, or preserving recoverability must distinguish something. When no additional operational distinction can be expressed without reintroducing distinction itself, the formal reduction reaches its expression boundary. This condition does not establish metaphysical nothingness, the ultimate physical nature of reality, or universal scientific completeness. It identifies the point at which the current formal system cannot generate a further meaningful operational distinction. A subsequently discovered material distinction may reopen the analysis. Meta-universal and recursive architecture The consolidated programme extends its governing principles to higher-order structures, including systems of systems, federated architectures, nested governance, adaptive frameworks, distributed representations, cross-domain dependencies, and evolving successor organizations. The meta-level framework treats the rules, evaluators, models, interfaces, verification processes, recovery resources, and governance mechanisms themselves as operational objects subject to examination. The intention is to prevent architectural changes, administrative classifications, technological substitutions, or recursive delegation from silently defeating the original recoverability requirements. The nine-dimensional expansion framework provides a finite combinatorial organization for exploring distinctions across orientation, time, roles, protected values, failures, responses, scope, evidence, and governance. Its combinatorial search space supports structured exploration and generation of test cases. It does not establish that every configuration is physically possible, scientifically novel, or empirically validated. Technical and computational applications The corpus includes material relating to processor-implemented operational determination, recoverability-constrained authorization, software and hardware continuity, input-output provenance, communication systems, distributed machine coordination, industrial transition isolation, artificial intelligence governance, financial continuity, healthcare systems engineering, water security, ecological systems, and other cross-domain research architectures. These applications share the principle of testing whether a proposed action preserves the necessary conditions for timely correction, restoration, substitution, containment, or admissible continuation. Where recoverability cannot be established, the proposed frameworks favour preserving a less irreversible state while additional evidence, authority, or corrective capacity is established. Legal, constitutional, and institutional dimensions The associated constitutional and governance materials propose principles concerning truthful distinction, human dignity, informed consent, legitimate authority, institutional responsibility, evidence preservation, accountable succession, restoration, and prevention of avoidable irreversible harm. These texts are proposed models for adoption and evaluation. Publication does not itself create binding national law, international treaty obligations, regulatory certification, or institutional adoption. Software and executable components The consolidated release preserves software-related material and research implementations associated with local corpus indexing, data integrity, evidence management, finite-state reachability, mathematical evaluation, and recoverability-oriented decision support. Individual implementations vary in completeness and validation status. Inclusion in this archive does not mean that every described architecture has been converted into a production-ready application or independently certified for safety-critical deployment. Archival construction and preservation This edition consists of nine ZIP volumes that preserve fifteen source archives from earlier Boundary consolidation and reconstruction releases. The preservation procedure retains historical versions and uses SHA-256 integrity verification to establish byte-level correspondence between the preserved source archives and their restored copies. An earlier damaged archive was also subjected to partial file-level recovery, with successfully recovered entries separated from unresolved source material. The present edition retains both earlier six-part releases and supplementary material rather than assuming that independently reconstructed archives are automatically complete substitutes for original source data. Verification and completeness boundaries This publication distinguishes four different forms of completeness: Archival integrity: verification that preserved source bytes match the corresponding recorded hashes. Finite formal completeness: exhaustive evaluation within explicitly defined finite states, transitions, constraints, and protected target classes. Implementation completeness: the extent to which specified functions have been implemented and successfully tested. Empirical completeness: the extent to which the model and its assumptions have been independently validated against actual operating conditions. Byte-level archival verification does not by itself prove semantic equivalence, operational correctness, scientific novelty, universal applicability, or completeness across all possible future systems. Real-world scientific, engineering, legal, and institutional applications require independent validation appropriate to their respective domains. Research significance The Boundary Project proposes a common language for examining how systems change while preserving materially necessary truth, identity, agency, responsibility, evidence, correction capacity, and recoverable future possibility. Its contribution as a research programme lies in bringing mathematical successor-state reasoning, temporal recoverability, technical control, institutional governance, and cross-domain continuity into one interoperable conceptual and computational framework. The programme invites formal analysis, independent replication, practical implementation, adversarial testing, domain-specific refinement, and comparative evaluation against existing methods in control theory, resilience engineering, safety, law, governance, and complex-systems research. Preservation and citation This Zenodo record should be cited as the consolidated nine-part preservation edition of the Boundary Project. Researchers should cite individual source publications or patent filings when referring to a specific theorem, technical disclosure, experiment, or legal instrument contained in the archive.
