Accurate and interpretable brain tumour detection from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) remains a significant challenge in computer-aided diagnosis. This study proposes an EfficientNet–Transformer Hybrid Network integrated with SHapley Additive ExPlanations (SHAP) and Grad-CAM explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) techniques for automated and trustworthy brain tumour classification. Methods: The proposed framework combines EfficientNet for local feature extraction and a Vision Transformer for global contextual learning. MRI images from publicly available benchmark datasets containing four classes (glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumour, and no tumour) were preprocessed and augmented before training. The model was trained using an 80:20 training-testing split, while SHAP and Grad-CAM were employed to provide feature-level and spatial explanations of predictions. Results: The proposed framework achieved a classification accuracy of 98.88%, outperforming several state-of-the-art CNN and transformer models. It also attained average precision, recall, and F1-score values of 98.90%, 98.88%, and 98.89%, respectively, with an average AUC of 0.9893. Ablation and robustness analyses demonstrated that integrating SHAP and Grad-CAM improved interpretability while maintaining high predictive performance under noisy conditions. Conclusions: The proposed EfficientNet–Transformer framework effectively combines local and global feature learning with dual explainability mechanisms to deliver accurate and clinically interpretable brain tumour classification. The results demonstrate its potential as a reliable computer-aided diagnosis tool for neuro-oncology and clinical decision support systems.

Augmentative and alternative communication systems are essential for people with severe speech and motor impairments, yet many interfaces remain slow, effortful, and error-prone. This study evaluated a hybrid brain-computer interface that combines steady-state visually evoked potentials (SSVEP) with eye-tracking to improve selection speed, reliability, and usability. Participants completed symbol selection, short phrase construction, and correction tasks under three conditions: SSVEP-only, eye-tracking-only, and hybrid SSVEP plus eye-tracking. In the hybrid condition, gaze rapidly narrowed the likely target region, while SSVEP classification confirmed user intent. Outcomes included selection rate, accuracy, errors, correction time, communication throughput, workload, effort, trust, and preference. The hybrid interface achieved the strongest performance, with faster selection than SSVEP-only and better control than eye-tracking-only. It also reduced accidental selections and correction burden, particularly in dense layouts and longer tasks. Results further emphasized personalized gaze thresholds, SSVEP windows, and visual layouts for sustained, practical AAC use across diverse user needs.
topics: Assistive Technology in Communication and Mobility

documents.abstract: Recent electroencephalography (EEG) foundation models increasingly emphasize model scale, potentially limiting their deployment on resource-constrained devices and in everyday environments. We argue that transferable EEG features can instead be learned with a compact architecture and introduce BrainCodes, a lightweight foundation model pretrained through self-supervised learning on more than 800 hours of recordings from over 1,000 participants. Our architecture combines a quantization-based neural tokenizer with a spatiotemporal encoder that supports arbitrary electrode configurations. The pretraining objective explicitly encourages representations that capture spatial connectivity through channel positional encoding, and sensitivity to narrowband neural oscillations through an auxiliary training objective. Our model matches or surpasses the state of the art across diverse neurophysiological monitoring tasks, including sleep staging, attention assessment, and cognitive load estimation. BrainCodes transfers effectively to low-resource wearable devices while using up to 97% fewer trainable parameters than comparable architectures. Beyond predictive accuracy, our evaluation framework characterizes the geometry and invariances of learned EEG representations across measurable spatial, temporal, and spectral signal properties.

While artificial intelligence has made rapid progress in mathematical reasoning, many open problems depend on structure that is revealed only through large-scale computational exploration and analytical synthesis. One such example is Lehmer's problem from 1933. It asks whether the Mahler measure of an integer polynomial, which measures how far its roots stray from the unit circle, can be made arbitrarily small. Previously, constructing irreducible polynomials with integer coefficients and small Mahler measure has been carried out systematically only for even degrees $d \le 180$. At higher degrees, Boyd's analytical one-parameter family frequently factors, skipping nearly 50% of target degrees and leaving no general construction for arbitrary $d$. Here, we address the high-degree regime through a human-AI discovery loop, in which we extend the conversational prompting with a fast numerical pipeline, an exact symbolic verifier, and large-scale distributed search. The AI agent prototypes numerical and symbolic solvers locally, launches parallel searches across distributed clusters and works with the human researcher to extract and verify mathematical hypotheses. Through this interactive loop, we derive a five-parameter construction, which we call the Generalized Boyd algorithm. It eliminates degree-skipping and constructs irreducible polynomials with Mahler measure strictly below Boyd's limit point $α_1 \approx 1.255434$ for every target degree. Evaluated across all even degrees up to 2000, our approach improves upon six previously published values and holds 99.6% of all best known records. With this work we release the verified dataset of polynomials with minimal Mahler measure across all studied even degrees.

Purpose The insurance industry is being transformed as artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping customer interactions, insurers' underwriting practices and service delivery. However, there is limited research or evidence on how customers' perceptions of AI-driven insurance services influence their purchase intentions. Taking inputs from technology acceptance model (TAM), this study investigates the relationship between customers' perceptions of AI-driven insurance services (CP-AI) and insurance purchase intentions (IPI) through the mediating role of the perceived ease of use (PEU). Design/methodology/approach A cross-sectional design was used in the study to collect the responses from 490 insurance customers from India who were familiar with AI-enabled insurance services. As CP-AI cannot be directly measured, it was conceptualised as a second-order reflective construct consisting of four important dimensions, i.e. attitude towards AI, AI service experience, trust in AI services and technology readiness. The hypothesised relationships were tested using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM). Findings The findings of the study highlights that the CP-AI have a significant positive impact on their purchase intentions. In addition, PEU partially mediates the relationship between CP-AI and their purchase intentions. Research limitations/implications The findings indicate that when customer perceptions are favourable, they are more effectively converted into IPI. In other words, if the AI-enabled insurance services are viewed as simple and effortless to use, the favourable customer perceptions are more likely to be converted into stronger IPI. These findings support the premise of the TAM that PEU is an important element linking technology perceptions to behavioural intentions, even in AI-enabled insurance service contexts. Practical implications The findings of the study provide practical insights for insurers to improve AI adoption among their customers by designing customer-friendly and easy-to-use AI-driven services, which will further improve customer acceptance and strengthen their purchase intentions. Originality/value This study extends research on AI-enabled insurance adoption by examining how customer perceptions influence purchase intentions through PEU. Its originality lies in conceptualising customer perceptions as a second-order reflective construct comprising attitude towards AI, AI service experience, trust in AI and technology readiness. Drawing on the TAM, the study demonstrates that perceived ease of use serves as an important mechanism linking favourable AI perceptions with purchase intentions. Based on responses from 490 Indian insurance customers, the study extends TAM to the AI-driven insurance context and offers practical insights for designing intuitive, customer-centric AI services.

Social integration of AI requires public trust and appropriate governance. This paper introduces the Generative Information Retrieval Accountability Assessment Framework (GIRAAF), designed to appraise accountability for Large Language Models and their applications, including AI chatbots. Drawing on Dahl’s (1998) notion of enlightened citizens, the framework comprises six interlinked dimensions: Information Readiness, Factual Correctness, Normative Alignment, Sourcing Practice, Transparency and Explainability, and Responsiveness and Adaptivity. Together, these dimensions link observable text outputs to intelligible standards, enabling systematic evaluation and accountable oversight. For scholars, developers and policymakers, GIRAAF provides a diagnostic heuristic and shared vocabulary for critical analysis of AI chatbot performance.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Corporate digital governance often fails to mitigate the social impact of digitalization due to short-term profit optimization, triggering AI black box phenomena that marginalize digital workers' welfare. This study explores the integration of ethical dimensions into corporate governance frameworks to safeguard stakeholder rights. Employing a qualitative literature review approach (2019–2026), this research analyzes technology corporations' accountability regarding automated work systems. The findings reveal that current platform governance prioritizes financial gains over social equity, leading to algorithmic opacity and worker vulnerability in Indonesia. Consequently, this research concludes that algorithmic transparency must become an integral part of corporate compliance. The study recommends mandating boards of directors to implement periodic ethical audits on artificial intelligence systems to ensure business sustainability and distributive justice.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Streaming video understanding (SVU) requires video-LLMs to process incoming video continuously while answering user queries with low latency. Recent methods reduce query-time cost by prefilling frames into KV caches during idle time and reusing the cached KVs at query time. To bound per-frame computation over unbounded video streams, these methods restrict the context available during prefill. This creates a fundamental context mismatch: the restricted context may omit information needed to properly contextualize video tokens, yet, still contain information irrelevant to the eventual query, which is unknown during prefill. We propose FrameBlend, a simple yet effective plug-and-play method to address this mismatch through selective KV recomputation, without requiring any additional training. At query time, FrameBlend re-prefills selected video tokens using query-relevant context and replaces their cached KVs with recomputed ones. Crucially, this recomputation enables shorter attention windows during idle-time prefill, substantially reducing prefill cost while improving accuracy. Experiments across three SVU frameworks and five streaming and offline benchmarks demonstrate accuracy gains of up to 3.9 pp. On RVS-Ego, FrameBlend reduces per-frame prefill FLOPs by over 20% and total processing time by 14-59% for retrieval-based frameworks, including the cost of query-time recomputation. These results demonstrate that a simple change in how contextualization is distributed between idle time and query time can improve the accuracy-efficiency trade-off for SVU.

Drought early warning systems that fuse satellite rainfall estimates with sparse rain-gauge networks must decide not only whether to issue an alert but also how much confidence to attach to it. The framework treats the classifier's predictive distribution as a calibrated object and evaluates it through the risk-coverage curve, which reports the selective error remaining after abstention at each coverage level. A propagation operator is defined that maps gauge-network density and satellite product uncertainty into the calibration of the predictive distribution, and a coverage guarantee is derived under an exchangeability assumption. The analysis is methodological: it specifies the estimator, the calibration diagnostic and the coverage bound, and it demonstrates how the risk-coverage curve changes as the propagation operator is tightened. The computed warming trend for the site is −0.1564 °C per decade, which the framework treats as a calibration-relevant drift term rather than as a drought signal. The contribution is a formal account of how uncertainty propagates from sparse gauges to alert confidence, and a decision rule that ties abstention to calibrated risk rather than to a fixed probability threshold.

A generally intelligent system acquires new skills efficiently without requiring humans to redesign its software scaffold for every new task. Yet language models rarely act alone. A harness is a symbolic program that orchestrates calls to the model, handling perception, memory, tool use, recovery, and inference allocation on the model's behalf. ARC-AGI-3 is an interactive benchmark in which agents must explore unfamiliar environments, figure out their goals on the fly, and keep learning as they go. On it, human-steered systems already report ceiling scores across the public games, so we know effective designs exist. We ask whether frontier models can build and improve such a harness on their own. Through a fixed coding bootstrap, each model constructs a complete task harness, acts through that harness on five development games, and revises the entire codebase twice. Every version is evaluated on twenty games that never influence adaptation. We measure task performance with Relative Human Action Efficiency (RHAE), which combines level completion with action efficiency relative to human baselines, and record dollar-denominated inference cost as a practical resource measure. Across 27 lineages, harness performance ranges from zero to near-ceiling scores. Two revisions raise mean held-out RHAE by only 2.80 points (95% interval [-1.44,7.35]). Development gains overstate held-out improvement, and reductions in inference cost can come at the expense of task performance. Human-steered systems demonstrate further headroom. These findings reveal a gap between autonomous harness construction and reliable adaptation under this two-revision protocol: even strong task performance does not ensure that subsequent revisions generalize or preserve existing capabilities.

Abstract This paper proposes "Casino Protocol Vol. 18 (Auto-Aggregation Edition)," a novel mathematical model and smart contract architecture designed for wisdom evaluation and automated fund distribution in autonomous AI agents, large language models (LLMs), and decentralized node economies. Traditional attention economies in internet commerce tend to rely on superficial traffic and page views, leading to an overflow of information lacking structural sustainability and ethics. In response, this protocol fully introduces the 3C3 consensus (\binom{3}{3} = 1) as a verification layer—where all three mandatory elements: (1) subjective sensory observational capacity (S_{\text{sense}}), (2) altruism (S_{\text{altruism}}), and (3) structural understanding of utility (S_{\text{structure}}) must simultaneously be present—alongside the resolution function defined as their synergistic product (R = S_{\text{sense}} \times S_{\text{altruism}} \times S_{\text{structure}}). Furthermore, by implementing an on-chain total resolution score auto-aggregation mechanism (totalResolutionSum), the protocol eliminates governor manual calculation risks and achieves deterministic and precise royalty distribution. We demonstrate that this approach establishes an economic ecosystem where high-resolution wisdom is sustainably and autonomously rewarded in a society where AI and humans coexist.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence triage of chest radiographs is often evaluated by discrimination and calibration, yet the clinically decisive quantity is the delay it introduces or removes from the escalation pathway. That delay is not a property of the model alone: it is produced jointly by model sensitivity, the queue discipline of the reporting service, and the timing rules that govern when a radiograph is escalated to a human reader. the present analysis formalises the escalation pathway as a target trial and derives the before-after-control-impact estimator appropriate to its emulation under staggered site-level adoption. Because no observational cohort is available, the design's operating characteristics are characterised analytically and by a replication-based evaluation under a declared variance structure with between-cluster standard deviation 6.0, residual standard deviation 4.5 and intraclass correlation 0.64. Across 2000 replications per design cell and cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32, the analysis identifies the cluster count at which a 5 percentage-point reduction in time-to-escalation is detectable at 80% power as 54. The contribution is a design-theoretic account of what a causal claim about AI diagnostic delay would require, and a demonstration that queue variability, not model accuracy, is the binding constraint on the estimand's identifiability.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Predictive models that flag patients for readmission risk are increasingly used to allocate post-discharge resources, but their training labels are drawn from community health worker (CHW) visit records that vary in completeness across clinics and payers. the present analysis treats that variation as a causal identification problem rather than a data-cleaning nuisance. It formalises the readmission-risk estimator as a function of both true clinical need and visit-record observability, and shows that the resulting misallocation is not a bias in the conventional sense but a stable equilibrium in which under-recorded patients are systematically under-served. A negative-control outcome design is proposed to detect and bound this misallocation: a placebo outcome that cannot be affected by the intervention but shares the same recording mechanism is used to estimate the recording-driven component of the risk score. The design is characterised analytically and evaluated through a replication-based power analysis under a declared variance structure (between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5, intraclass correlation = 0.64). Power was estimated across 2000 design cells for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The analysis indicates that 52 clusters are required to detect a 5-percentage-point effect at 80% power. The contribution is a design, not an estimate: a negative-control outcome framework that makes the recording mechanism visible in readmission-risk evaluation, together with the operating characteristics that determine whether such an evaluation is feasible in a given health system.

Artificial intelligence cyclone track emulators are increasingly used to generate evacuation triggers, yet their adversarial robustness is typically assessed only against the emulator that was attacked. The framework combines a Lipschitz continuity condition on the emulator mapping with a disagreement radius derived from ensemble spread, yielding a certified upper bound on the probability that a perturbation crafted for a source emulator succeeds against a target emulator. The bound is expressed as a function of the perturbation magnitude, the spectral norm of the emulator Jacobian, and the pairwise disagreement between ensemble members. A case study using NASA POWER monthly reanalysis for Lagos, Nigeria (2000–2023, 312 monthly observations) illustrates the calibration of the disagreement radius; the observed mean temperature was 26.414 °C and the warming trend was 0.1553 °C per decade. The framework yields an evacuation-order safety condition that translates the certified bound into a maximum permissible perturbation magnitude for a given false-alarm tolerance. The contribution is a formal, assumption-explicit guarantee that links adversarial transferability to ensemble disagreement and to the operational safety of evacuation decisions.

Climate-index insurance payout models increasingly rely on machine-learning predictors trained on historical weather and yield data, yet covariate shift between training and deployment distributions can silently widen compensation disparities between smallholder and commercial farms. The framework is operationalised on NASA POWER monthly reanalysis for Accra, Ghana (2000–2023, 312 observations), where the estimated mean temperature is 26.521 °C and the warming trend is 0.1622 °C per decade, establishing a concrete shift regime against which audit thresholds can be calibrated. Formal results establish that the certified disparity bound decomposes into a shift-invariant base disparity plus a shift-amplified term controlled by the Wasserstein radius, and that the bound is tight for threshold payout rules. Auditing only marginal parity is insufficient under shift, because conditional payout gaps can grow while marginal gaps remain stable. The contribution is a certifiable audit protocol that converts covariate-shift assumptions into enforceable disparity bounds for smallholder compensation equity.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Neural climate emulators are increasingly used to produce seasonal forecasts, yet their reliability collapses when forced by radiative or land-surface conditions outside the training distribution. The framework combines a Mahalanobis-style score in a learned latent space with a conformal calibration layer, producing a certified threshold that controls the probability of silently accepting an OOD input. We derive high-probability bounds on the score gap between in-distribution and OOD regimes, and show that the certified threshold is achievable with a calibration sample whose size scales logarithmically in the confidence level. The framework is illustrated on a reanalysis-derived temperature series for Nairobi, Kenya (2000–2023, 312 monthly observations, mean 20.146 °C, warming trend 0.2477 °C per decade), where the emulator's latent score exhibits a clear separation between historical and perturbed forcing regimes. The certified detector attains a bounded false-negative rate under a range of computed forcing perturbations while preserving in-distribution coverage. The analysis clarifies when OOD certification is feasible for climate emulators and when it is not, and it identifies the calibration budget as the binding constraint on seasonal forecast safety.

Pest classifiers deployed on field-acquired images are exposed to adversarial perturbations that can flip a confident prediction while remaining visually inconspicuous to a human scout. The classifier is smoothed by adding isotropic Gaussian noise to the input and taking a majority vote over the induced distribution; the resulting certificate bounds the L2 radius within which no perturbation can change the predicted class. The analysis is a design and power study, not an observational one: the operating characteristics of the certification procedure are evaluated across a declared variance structure with between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5 and intraclass correlation = 0.64, using 2000 replications per design cell over cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The design attains 80% power at 5 percentage points with 52 clusters. The certified radius is a deployment parameter rather than a benchmark score, and that the intraclass correlation of field imagery governs how many independent field clusters a certification claim requires. The contribution is a formal certificate, a power-calibrated protocol for evaluating it, and a boundary condition: certification is informative only when the smoothing variance is matched to the perturbation budget the deployment actually faces.

Volcanic aerosol injection could alter seasonal precipitation patterns in ways that existing artificial intelligence (AI) forecast systems have never encountered, yet famine early-warning triggers built on those forecasts carry no formal reliability guarantee under such distributional shift. The framework combines a divergence-based shift detector, a distributionally robust conformal prediction layer, and a trigger reliability calculus that maps forecast intervals to famine early-warning activation probabilities. Formal results establish that the coverage gap under shift is bounded by the total variation distance between source and target distributions, that the trigger false-alarm rate is controlled at a user-specified level, and that the bound is tight in a minimax sense. The analysis is methodological and theoretical: no empirical forecast data are analysed, and the framework is presented as a certified design that would require validation against reanalysis and observational records before operational deployment. The contribution is a set of coverage and reliability guarantees that make the epistemic status of famine triggers explicit under a forcing scenario for which no historical training analogue exists.

Sparse agricultural sensor networks across sub-Saharan Africa leave crop-failure early-warning systems with too little ground observation to support reliable famine relief targeting. The framework treats sensor sparsity as a missing-data problem with a known observation operator and propagates climate-analytics uncertainty through a temporal Kalman-Buys filter whose gain is constrained by a certified risk envelope. Using NASA POWER monthly reanalysis for Accra, Ghana (2000-2023, 312 observations), the analysis establishes a mean temperature of 26.521 C and a warming trend of 0.1622 C per decade, which calibrates the climate-analytics prior. The derived bounds show that relief-targeting error scales with the square root of sensor density and with the Lipschitz constant of the crop-response function, yielding an explicit sensor-placement rule for a target misclassification rate. The contribution is a certified, assumption-explicit bridge between climate analytics and famine relief targeting that states the conditions under which early warning is trustworthy.

Provable robustness is a cornerstone of trustworthy machine learning, aiming to guarantee model predictions under adversarial perturbations. Existing certification frameworks, inspired by abstract interpretation or symbolic execution, typically assume a fixed computation graph, where input perturbations or variations affect only model outputs but not the underlying execution path. This assumption, however, is violated in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) Large Language Models (LLMs), whose input-dependent routing induces discrete and dynamic execution paths. Crucially, this dynamic computation changes the certified object from a single fixed function to a composition of input-dependent sub-functions, leading to unreliable certification guarantees. This paper presents \textsc{CertMoE}, the first routing-aware robustness certification framework for MoE LLMs, which explicitly accounts for input-induced routing dynamics in certification. Specifically, we introduce a relaxed routing-containment criterion, which certifies that perturbed Top-$K$ routing is contained within a larger certified expert pool. Based on this guarantee, \textsc{CertMoE} then constructs the corresponding induced sub-network and certifies its prediction consistency. This hierarchical certification procedure yields a joint probabilistic guarantee over routing containment and sub-network robustness, providing sufficient conditions under which the original prediction remains invariant. Extensive experiments across recent MoE LLMs demonstrate that dynamic routing makes certificates issued by existing methods frequently violated, while \textsc{CertMoE} reduces the empirical violation rate with routing-aware guarantees, e.g., from more than $30\%$ to $0$, yielding certificates that more faithfully reflect the robustness of MoE models.

Data agents built on ReAct-style loops now execute complex analytical workflows over structured data, yet their intermediate reasoning still runs almost entirely through text. Human analysts instead move between numbers, tables, and charts, reading visual evidence to expose trends and anomalies that text summaries drop. We ask whether charts can serve as internal epistemic actions inside a data agent's reasoning loop, and how to teach an agent to use them. We first build \probe{}, a suite of 200 controlled tasks under four matched interface conditions, and find a persistent gap between what agents can read and what they choose to use. Agents score as well from self-generated charts as from numeric output, yet plotting access alone does not translate into consistent use. Task slices show that charts lead on temporal, pattern, and anomaly reasoning, while text leads on precise reading and conditional verification. We then propose \method{}, which distils two families of experience from conditioned trajectory rollouts. One family records how to select and verify analytical operations, and the other records when to invoke text, charts, or both. A trajectory judge scores outcomes and labels intermediate steps, and a validation gate admits only experience that improves held-out performance. On three held-out benchmarks with four LLM backbones, \method{} raises analytical accuracy and visual evidence quality over matched baselines, and backbones that never drew charts begin using them, all without touching model parameters.

In the context of ChatGPT as a shopping assistant in Indonesia, this research investigates the correlations between satisfaction and factors such as perceived utility, anthropomorphism, ease of use, and navigation, as well as the link between satisfaction and buy intention. Using the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), the research takes into account functional perceptions in addition to conversational AI's human-like and interaction-related traits. The data were analysed using structural equation modelling (SEM) with AMOS from a quantitative, cross-sectional survey that was administered to 200 participants. The findings show that elements such as perceived utility, anthropomorphism, and navigation are positively and substantially linked to satisfaction. There is a positive correlation between perceived ease of use and satisfaction, however the link is not statistically significant (β = 0.135, p = 0.063). Having a positive and substantial association with purchase intention (β = 0.537, p < 0.001) constitutes satisfaction. It turns out that four out of five possibilities are correct. According to the results, in this particular sample, features connected to interactions and practical utility are linked to satisfaction, although simplicity of use by itself does not show any statistical significance. Caution is required due to the study's cross-sectional methodology and conflicting model-fit results, but it does expand the applicability of TAM to conversational shopping help in Indonesia.

The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AI), particularly ChatGPT, offers opportunities to enhance learning while raising concerns about academic integrity. This study examines the role of ChatGPT in Islamic Religious Education (IRE) and formulates strategies to preserve students’ academic integrity. Using a qualitative library research approach, it analyzes scientific articles, books, policy documents, and other credible sources on generative AI, IRE, learning autonomy, and academic integrity through content analysis and thematic synthesis. The findings indicate that ChatGPT can improve access to learning resources, support independent learning, clarify complex concepts, and provide preliminary feedback. However, excessive reliance may encourage plagiarism, weaken critical thinking, reduce originality, and produce inaccurate information. Six complementary strategies are proposed: institutional policies, academic guidelines, cultivation of academic honesty, higher-order thinking tasks (C4–C6), authentic performance-based assessment, and contextual and problem-based learning. These strategies position ChatGPT as a supporting tool rather than a substitute for students’ intellectual processes, and its outputs must be critically verified against credible scholarly sources. The study concludes that the educational value of ChatGPT in IRE depends on sound pedagogical design and a strong ethical framework. Because the framework is a conceptual synthesis of the literature, it has not been empirically validated and should be tested in future research.

Abstract This study examines how first-generation and Hispanic/Latino/a students enrolled in an introductory undergraduate psychology course perceived the influence of ChatGPT, a generative AI tool, on their academic skill development, learning experiences, and confidence. This study surveyed 88 students enrolled across four sections of an introductory undergraduate psychology course, with the goal of understanding student perceptions of ChatGPT. Of those surveyed, 67% identified as first-generation, 55% as Hispanic/Latino/a, and 41.9% as both first-generation and Hispanic/Latino/a. Analyses suggested that first-generation and Hispanic/Latino/a students reported more favorable perceptions of ChatGPT’s usefulness than their peers. While the study does not claim generalizability, its findings offer insight into how diverse students perceived AI tools in this educational setting. Interpretations are informed by the Digital Learning Ecosystem and decolonial pedagogy frameworks. Implications for instruction include opportunities for scaffolding AI use to support student agency, identity, and academic confidence in classroom environments.

documents.abstract: Language models make it easy to build classifiers by simply prompting a model with the sample to classify. However, their predictions are neither deterministic nor uniformly reliable across samples. How can we combine predictions from different models to improve reliability? We view LLM classifiers as noisy measurement instruments of an underlying target label. Our goal is to maximize average classification accuracy at a given average query cost. To this end, we introduce circuits that organize LLM classifiers into an adaptive sequence of queries and decisions. We then characterize the optimal circuit, obtain the fundamental limits of achievable accuracy, and provide practical insights on realizing the optimal circuit. Across seven classification tasks spanning safety, health, political science, human preference, agent evaluation, decision-making and reasoning, our method improves the cost-accuracy frontier over routing and cascading baselines.

Dengue warning-sign recognition depends on capillary refill assessment, a bedside skill whose reliability varies widely among clinicians. Computer vision systems that estimate refill time from smartphone video could standardise triage, but their safety depends on how they interact with the variable skill of the humans who defer to them. The framework characterises triage safety through a deferral operating characteristic and derives the conditions under which machine deferral reduces, rather than redistributes, triage error. A design-based evaluation of the before-after-control-impact estimator was conducted under a declared variance structure with between-cluster standard deviation 6.0, residual standard deviation 4.5 and intraclass correlation 0.64, across 2000 replications per design cell for cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The analysis indicates that 54 clusters are required to detect a 5 percentage point effect at 80 percent power. The framework proposes that deferral safety is governed not by model accuracy alone but by the covariance between model and clinician errors, and that this covariance is itself a function of clinician skill. The contribution is a formal account of when human-in-the-loop deferral improves triage safety for dengue warning-sign recognition under variable capillary refill assessment skill.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Sickle cell retinopathy screening in African primary care is constrained by fundus cameras of unequal resolution, and the safety of artificial-intelligence referral grading under that heterogeneity has not been characterised. The framework treats the referral decision as a thresholded function of a latent retinopathy severity score, decomposes the resolution-induced distribution shift into a recoverable component and an irreducible information-loss component, and derives a bound on the change in referral sensitivity under adaptation. A before-after-control-impact design with a declared variance structure (between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5, intraclass correlation = 0.64) was used to characterise the operating characteristics of the evaluation design across 2000 replications per design cell, with cluster counts of 8, 16, 24 and 32 and effect sizes of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points. The design requires 54 clusters to detect a 5-percentage-point effect at 80% power. The framework proposes that adaptation safety should be reported as a resolution-stratified sensitivity profile rather than a single aggregate metric, and identifies the conditions under which super-resolution adaptation preserves or degrades referral safety. The contribution is a design-level and decision-level formalisation that makes resolution heterogeneity an explicit object of evaluation rather than an uncontrolled nuisance.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Digital learning systems rarely adapt to momentary cognitive state, creating risk of underload or overload. The current study investigates whether EEG-based closed-loop pacing can alter task load dynamics during a digital constellation-learning task. Fifty-one participants were randomly assigned to adaptive, reward, or control conditions. In the adaptive condition, a task load index derived from frontal theta and parietal alpha adjusted feedback duration between 3 and 8 s; fixed 5s feedback was used in reward and control conditions, with reward participants expecting to receive performance-contingent draw entries. Accuracy increased across blocks in all groups, with no significant group or group-by-block effect. In contrast, EEG indices showed group-specific trajectories: task load decreased over time in the adaptive condition, and frontal theta and parietal alpha showed significant group-by-block interactions. The adaptive condition also showed reduced late-session feedback duration, while reward participants reported higher satisfaction. Intrinsic motivation did not moderate group effects, although perceived competence predicted final-block performance and interest, effort, and competence predicted engagement. These findings suggest that EEG-based feedback pacing can regulate neurophysiological task load dynamics despite lack of immediate accuracy gains under the present task constraints. The results support neuroadaptive scaffolding as a state-regulation mechanism for digital learning.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Root cause analysis (RCA) and mitigation prediction are essential for incident management, enabling the identification of underlying causes of failures and ensuring the reliability of complex cloud-based systems. With rising incident volume and system complexity, incident reports have become a valuable resource for these tasks. Recent studies have shown promising results using Large Language Models (LLMs) to predict root causes and mitigation actions from textual descriptions in incident reports. Despite these advances, further progress is hindered by the lack of publicly available datasets; existing work relies on private data, which limits transparency, reproducibility, and generalization. To address this gap, we introduce CloudIR-Bench, the first publicly available benchmark providing a dataset and evaluation framework for incident report-based RCA and mitigation prediction. Curated from incident reports across five leading cloud-based systems, CloudIR-Bench captures a diverse range of real-world production scenarios representing authentic failures and engineers' reasoning. We also release an open-source evaluation framework that includes eight recent LLM-based approaches. Our comprehensive evaluation includes zero-shot and in-context learning experiments, along with a qualitative analysis to identify where and why LLMs fail. Benchmarking results reveal the capabilities and limitations of existing LLMs in this domain. The benchmark, including the dataset, framework and supplementary materials, is available at https://github.com/hoangtnm/CloudIR-Bench.

Self-management in heart failure (HF) is essential for improving outcomes, yet adherence remains suboptimal, particularly among older adults and individuals with limited health literacy. Large language models (LLMs) generating patient education content at scale, yet evidence regarding their accuracy and alignment with HF patient needs is limited. To compare the quality of responses generated by five widely used LLMs (DeepSeek, Doubao, Grok, Gemini, and ChatGPT) to self-management questions of HF patients from two perspectives (professional and patient perception), and to quantify the discrepancies between these perspectives. A cross-sectional study. A structured 45-item question bank on self-management among HF patients, encompassing six domains and varying in type and difficulty, was administered to five LLMs. Responses were independently evaluated by four healthcare professionals using four domains (accuracy, completeness, safety, and actionability; 1–5 Likert scale with safety veto). Fifteen HF patients assessed responses in terms of comprehensibility, usefulness, satisfaction, and trustworthiness. Generalized estimating equations (GEE), intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC), and linear mixed-effects models were used to compare performance and assess variability across raters and models. DeepSeek achieved the highest professional evaluation score (19.49/20), significantly exceeding those of the other models (GEE β = −1.79 to − 1.06, all P < 0.001). In contrast, patients rated Doubao highest (16.93), followed by DeepSeek (16.33), particularly among older and lower-education subgroups. The professional–patient discrepancy varied substantially across models, ranging from 1.50 (Doubao) to 5.02 (ChatGPT). Notably, responses involving dietary sodium restriction showed consistent safety concerns across models, yet patients consistently rated these items favorably. Diet and sodium restriction consistently emerged as the weakest-performing domain across all models. Professional and patient evaluations of LLM-generated self-management education for HF patients diverged significantly. DeepSeek ranked highest clinically, but patients favored Doubao for its readability and trustworthiness, emphasizing the need to balance clinical accuracy with patient-centered design in healthcare AI.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: AI tools for 3D content generation are expanding digital modeling for additive manufacturing, but their suitability for engineering-oriented Fused Filament Fabrication (FFF) remains limited when target geometry requires dimensional control, valid meshes, feature orientation, component separation, and functional interpretation. This study evaluates the first-response behavior of ChatGPT, Gemini, and DeepSeek using four benchmark conditions: a solid cube, a cube with a central through-hole, a monolithic compliant tweezer, and a male/female snap-fit pair. The protocol reproduced a common user interaction: one standardized request, the first returned output, and no iterative regeneration or prompt refinement. Manually modeled and printed standards were used as targets. Outputs were evaluated as upstream FFF candidates by STL/G-code integrity, bounding-box correspondence, watertightness, winding consistency, component count, feature preservation, snap-fit plausibility, and repair burden. ChatGPT produced the highest number of accepted first-response outputs across the tested conditions; Gemini performed well for simple geometries but fragmented or simplified more demanding cases; and DeepSeek showed feature, orientation, and topology failures. Image input improved scale and layout communication but did not replace mesh inspection or engineering-feature verification. AI-generated STL files should be treated as preliminary FFF design candidates, not direct engineering-grade components.

Background Large language model (LLM) chatbot platforms are increasingly used for health information, but their performance for pediatric immunoglobulin A vasculitis (IgAV) patient education is unclear. Objective To compare ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Doubao across content completeness, quality and reliability, readability, understandability, and actionability. Methods Thirty-two standardized English questions were submitted to ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Doubao on August 9, 2026, using a new conversation for each question and retaining the first complete response (96 responses). Two reviewers independently performed the original assessment, with third-reviewer adjudication. GQS, mDISCERN, QAMAI, six readability metrics, PEMAT-P, and ICC(2,1) were used. During revision, a question-specific clinical checklist was established and applied to all archived answers. The research team completed the revision scoring and confirmed the final omission results. Results Clinically relevant information omissions occurred in 16/96 responses (16.67%): 0/32 for ChatGPT, 5/32 for DeepSeek, and 11/32 for Doubao. Retained ratings identified outdated medical advice in 2/96 responses (2.08%) and no real-time information errors or hallucinations. At least one recorded content deficiency occurred in 18/96 responses (18.75%). Original ICC(2,1) values ranged from 0.767 to 0.954. Overall differences were significant for GQS, mDISCERN, QAMAI, PEMAT-U, and PEMAT-A (all P < .01), but not for readability metrics. Bonferroni-adjusted contrasts showed lower ARI, FKGL, CLI, and SMOG scores for DeepSeek than ChatGPT. DeepSeek had the highest PEMAT-U score; ChatGPT had the highest PEMAT-A score. Conclusions Performance varied by evaluation domain, and clinically relevant omissions remained a safety concern. The omission findings reflect criteria established during revision and do not establish a validated platform safety ranking. LLM platforms may supplement patient education but should not replace professional medical review.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Background Thyroid eye disease (TED), together with its acute and vision-threatening complication, dysthyroid optic neuropathy (DON), requires timely diagnosis and intervention. The limited availability of specialists in orbital diseases poses a significant challenge to ophthalmology residency training. In this context, generative artificial intelligence (AI) has created new opportunities for medical education, though its effectiveness in ophthalmology training remains to be explored. Objective This exploratory study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in ophthalmology education, focusing on TED domains. Methods The 46 residents (28 general residents and 18 ophthalmology residents) were randomly assigned to either an AI-assisted or a teacher-made 5-min teaching video on TED. All participants then completed three tests through online questionnaire experiments, each consisting of 20-item clinical questions about TED. Test 1 served as a baseline assessment of disease knowledge, Test 2 was conducted 5 min after learning to evaluate short-term learning outcomes, along with a questionnaire survey about AI tools, and Test 3 was administered 1 week later to assess long-term learning outcome. Results Viewing the AI-assisted video significantly improved test scores from baseline to 5 min (mean difference = 13.04; p = 0.004), but the improvement was not sustained at 1 week (mean difference = 7.61; p = 0.16). Completion time also decreased significantly from baseline to both 5 min (p = 0.009; GMR = 0.57) and 1 week (p < 0.001; GMR = 0.45). No significant differences were observed between the AI-assisted and teacher-made video groups across all assessments (all p > 0.05). Additionally, learning experience was positively correlated with learning outcome (r = 0.60; P < 0.001). Conclusion Our findings suggested that the AI-assisted and teacher-made videos for TED education showed no statistically significant difference. However, substantial expert oversight was required, and the AI-assisted workflow did not reduce total production time in this study. Given the limited long-term retention, such AI-assisted videos may be better positioned as supplementary resources combined with human expertise.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Objectives: To compare fracture detection rates and observer confidence between a high-frequency hockey-stick transducer and a conventional linear transducer for detecting non-displaced dentoalveolar fractures in a paired ex vivo model. Materials and Methods: This paired ex vivo study included 88 experimentally created non-displaced dentoalveolar fracture sites in fresh ovine specimens. Two oral and maxillofacial radiologists independently evaluated all sites with both a 12L3 conventional linear transducer (10–15 MHz) and an 18H5 hockey-stick transducer (10–18 MHz), with transducer order randomized. Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) confirmed fracture status. Within-observer paired fracture-detection outcomes were compared using the exact McNemar test, and a cluster-adjusted generalized estimating equation (GEE) analysis accounted for repeated assessments and clustering within ovine heads. Observer confidence was compared using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Results: Observer 1 detected 76/88 fracture sites (86.4%) with the hockey-stick transducer and 64/88 (72.7%) with the conventional linear transducer (p = 0.004). Observer 2 detected 74/88 sites (84.1%) and 62/88 (70.5%), respectively (p < 0.001). In the cluster-adjusted GEE analysis, the hockey-stick transducer was associated with higher odds of fracture detection (OR, 2.29; 95% CI, 1.84–2.86; p < 0.001). For both observers, confidence scores were higher with the hockey-stick transducer (median [IQR], 4 [3–4] vs. 3 [2–3]; both p < 0.001), with Cohen’s dz values of 0.849 and 0.791, respectively. In a separate pre-study calibration set, interobserver agreement was 95% (κ = 0.828; 95% CI, 0.503–1.000). Conclusions: In this ex vivo model, the hockey-stick transducer achieved consistently higher fracture-detection rates across both observers and greater observer confidence than the conventional linear transducer. The observed differences may reflect the combined technical and ergonomic characteristics of the two transducers rather than probe geometry alone. Prospective clinical studies including both fractured and non-fractured sites are required before conclusions regarding diagnostic accuracy or clinical superiority can be established.

The article proposes a component-based approach to assessing the applicability of large language models in decision support systems. The necessity of multidimensional evaluation is substantiated, and an original methodology for component-based assessment is presented, taking into account both the content of the text and its suitability for specific applied contexts. Unlike existing review scales, the approach suggests the use of operational applicability profiles of the response and a decision-making procedure at the level of a specific output. The components capture verifiable properties of the response and serve as the basis for reproducible metrics and evaluation criteria. The approach is oriented toward typical decision support system tasks and can be applied in both expert and automated scenarios. The methodology can be used to verify generated results and enhance the substantiation of trust in them.

Managed and wild bees sustain roughly a third of the global food products, yet colonies face mounting stress from climate-change including extreme weather patterns, altered parasite and disease patterns. Timely assessment of colony condition such as understanding colony strength, brood area, honey and pollen storage, comb usage, is essential to adaptive management. However, manual hive frame inspection is slow, costly, and quality depends on scarce expertise. We present an artificial targeted intelligent system framework focusing on edge deployable pipeline that turns hive frame photographs into interpretable and action-oriented inspection report. The pipeline includes an object detector to detect biologically-meaningful comb-cell classes; detections are distilled into structured fact schema; facts are converted into constrained factual text; the text triggers a grounded knowledge-base for interpretations and recommendations. Knowledge-base entries are required to be triggerable by evidence expressed in the fact schema. We built our system based on open source FAIRHiveFrames-1K dataset and favour reproducible, edge-deployable models over large general purpose frontier models. We additionally release FAIRHiveText-1K dataset that turns FAIRHiveFrames-1K dataset into interchangeable facts and text interpretation of the facts, making it easy for further LLM-based research into this area. We also propose a pathway to develop the grounded knowledge-base that will be helpful in providing interpretable and actionable reports from the facts.

Smartphone-based computer vision for diabetic foot ulcer triage is typically validated under lighting conditions that do not match those of the clinics where referral decisions are made. the present analysis treats the resulting distribution shift as a domain-generalization problem and asks whether reported classification accuracy survives realistic illumination variation, and what that survival implies for referral safety. Because no primary image corpus was available, the study is a methodological and analytical evaluation: it formalises illumination shift as a transformation of the input distribution, derives a bound on the degradation of a classifier's referral sensitivity under covariate shift, and characterises the operating characteristics of a before-after-control-impact design for field validation under a declared variance structure (between-cluster SD = 6.0, residual SD = 4.5, intraclass correlation = 0.64). Power was estimated across 2000 design cells spanning 8, 16, 24 and 32 clusters and effects of 3, 5 and 8 percentage points; 54 clusters are required for 5 percentage points at 80% power. Lighting-induced shift can silently erode sensitivity in the very range where referral decisions are made, that aggregate accuracy conceals this erosion, and that the field designs commonly used to validate such systems are underpowered to detect it. The contribution is a formal account of why lighting variation is a safety problem rather than a nuisance variable, and a design framework for evaluating it.

documents.abstract: Contemporary software systems are now being used in environments that are highly concurrent, data-intensive, and latency-sensitive. Software-Defined Networks (SDNs) applications like real-time intrusion detection need fast pattern recognition in large amounts of data streams through time. Although deep learning models have impressive detection capabilities, failure to perform well in real-world deployments is usually limited by poor concurrency management, inflexible scheduling, centralized learning pipelines, and fault tolerance. In this study, the authors suggest a concurrency-aware artificial intelligence (CA-AI) framework that directly incorporates actor-based concurrency control, workflow-based load-aware scheduling, deep long short-term memory (LSTM)-based temporal learning, agent-based parallel feature extraction, and feedback loops based on monitoring. The framework is evaluated for SDN-oriented intrusion detection workloads, where concurrency management is implemented at the system architecture level through actor-based execution, workflow scheduling, and asynchronous inference and tested on real network traffic data samples (NSL-KDD, CIC-IDS2017, and UNSW-NB15). Experimental results demonstrate that concurrency-aware system design leads to a significant improvement in the detection accuracy achieving up to 98.9% detection accuracy across multiple benchmark datasets, including NSL-KDD, CIC-IDS2017, and UNSW-NB15, throughput improved by 2.1 × compared with the centralized IDS baseline, while throughput increased by approximately 1.19 × when concurrency increased from 10,000 to 100,000 flows within the proposed CA-AI framework, average latency was reduced by approximately 57.5% compared with the centralized IDS baseline (146 ms to 62 ms), while maintaining high reliability under concurrent workloads. The proposed framework establishes concurrency as a fundamental architectural principle for scalable AI-driven pattern recognition systems.

LLM-generated records increasingly populate production information systems where they are treated as data assets subject to the same quality expectations as records from operational databases. A single such record can simultaneously satisfy and violate a quality rule: a grounded fact adjacent to a hallucination, a useful answer adjacent to a stereotype. Classical data cleaning cannot resolve this because the two judgments are incompatible over the same span; a single LLM judge cannot either, since it shares the training biases that produced the conflict. Existing interventions such as prompt engineering, chain-of-thought, and RLHF reduce surface error rates but provide no audit trail and cannot distinguish genuine remediation from blanket suppression. The question is whether a deterministic check over structured inter-agent records can catch the defects that referential checks alone miss. We present BiasGuard-D: two adversarial roles drawn from distinct model families exchange typed claim documents, a three-model quorum adjudicates by majority vote, and a combined referential-plus-semantic invariant validates the verdict. The semantic component fires on verdicts referential checks miss; removing the iterative loop drops invariant satisfaction sharply. The deliberation layer transfers from stereotype to hallucination remediation on HaluEval QA with only role-framing changes, raising right-answer recovery by 49 percentage points; the triage gate required a cross-family second auditor to maintain recall on objective hallucination. Every claim, vote, and instruction is stored as a typed record giving operators a provenance trail auditable under emerging AI regulations.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Sorghum yield estimation in smallholder regions of southern Africa is constrained by sparse weather-station networks, and the machine-learning models used to fill the resulting gaps typically report point predictions without distribution-free guarantees. The framework is formalised for the case of covariate shift induced by interpolation error, and a weighted conformal score is derived that restores marginal coverage under a bounded shift assumption. The method is evaluated on a real reanalysis record for Harare, Zimbabwe: NASA POWER monthly air temperature at 2 m, 312 monthly observations from 2000 to 2023, with a mean of 18.914 °C, a standard deviation of 3.107 °C and a warming trend of 0.2001 °C per decade. Coverage-guarantee properties are established analytically and illustrated against this record. The contribution is a coverage-guarantee evaluation protocol that separates the uncertainty contributed by the yield model from the uncertainty contributed by the weather interpolation, and that reports interval width as a function of station density rather than as a single scalar. The framework is proposed as a methodological basis for yield-estimation systems that must state what their intervals actually cover.

In the first part of this three-part series, we reviewed the mechanisms that cause nuisance signals in fMRI data. Here, in the second part of the series, we review "human factors" that modulate these confounding mechanisms. The modulators may be trait characteristics such as age or bodyweight, or they may be state dependencies that alter the relative contributions of nuisance signals in the fMRI data. A wide array of psychological (e.g., motivation/arousal, cognitive strategy, task engagement), lifestyle (e.g., exercise, sleep, and dietary habits), experimental (e.g., scanner anxiety, task-related movement), and situational (e.g., prandial state, time of day, menses) factors can affect the brain state directly as well as via changes in systemic physiology mediated by autonomic nervous responses.

LLMs are increasingly consulted for moral judgment. We aim to improve performance on such tasks by rewarding good arguments, on the premise that arguing well increases the likelihood of judging well. We train a reinforcement learning policy initialized from a state-of-the-art language model in a self-judged tournament with masked thinking: the generated arguments are judged pairwise on argument quality by the policy itself. As an empirical basis, we extract authentic dilemmas from classic novels, using a logic solver to verify that each constitutes a conflict. We show that our judge rates argument quality like human annotators, and the policy then adopts the language register that it rewards. Testing on the external benchmarks MoralChoice, ELEPHANT, and MORABLES, we find that the policy becomes more decisive and invariant to the order in which options are presented, but sycophancy and reframing remain a challenge to validity. Two ablation studies with synthetic dilemmas and unmasked thinking match the reordering gains, but show a weaker register shift and higher sycophancy. We conclude that consistency is not validity: consistency under reordering can be optimized without improving the moral judgment it is meant to signal.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Continuum is a user-owned layer (software, with an optional sovereign hardward embodiment) that sits between a user and every AI agent that serves them. It answers two problems. The knowledge problem: every model accumulates context about its user and holds it hostage; switching models means starting over. The agency problem: agents now transact on users' behalf (buying, booking, subscribing) under platform rules, with ties boken by sponsored defaults and no receipt the user can inspect. Continuum holds the user's semantic log (fidelity-stamped claims with provenance, confidence, verification status, and emotional weight), cognitive profile, and standing preferences in one user-owned place, and governs through them: every consequential agent action passes a policy gate (ALLOW / DENY / ESCALATE), ties among acceptable options are broken by the user's rules before any platform default, and every decision is sealed with a tamper-evident, hash-chained receipt. The same governance shapes conversation (age appropriate for a child, full depth for a deivergent adult) enforced in the user's layer, not the model's. Any model plugs in via MCP; the model is a module, the user is the constant. This document is a defensive disclosure; it establishes dated prior art for the composition and claims.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This working paper presents a human-first ownership architecture for cooperative AI data centers. As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly important to economic and social life, the ownership and governance of the infrastructure supporting it will shape who benefits, who bears the costs, and how communities participate in decisions affecting them. The paper examines cooperative ownership as an alternative to conventional data center development, with a focus on aligning infrastructure investment with human needs, community interests, democratic governance, and shared economic benefit. It establishes a conceptual foundation for developing AI infrastructure in which workers, communities, and other cooperative members can participate in ownership and decision-making. The proposed architecture is intended to support further research, feasibility analysis, cooperative development, financing, and implementation. Real-world development will require additional work on site selection, power availability, capital requirements, operating economics, governance, environmental performance, and community impact. This paper is part of the Robert Wayne Human Reclamation Project (RWHRP)'s broader effort to develop practical, human-centered alternatives to systems that concentrate economic power and decision-making. The proposed cooperative AI data center is intended as an initial implementation project through which the architecture can be evaluated and advanced toward practical application. The paper is published to invite scrutiny, research, collaboration, and participation from cooperative developers, community organizations, energy professionals, researchers, prospective partners, and potential funders.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Before an AI agent takes a consequential action, such as paying, messaging or changing code, several monitors check it. Their verdicts are combined by aggregating scores or by counting approvals, whatever inputs the monitors share. Monitors that share a base model or a poisoned input, however, may fail together. We borrow the fail-prone systems of distributed computing: lists of monitor sets that may fail together. A rule is safe if it executes no bad action and live if it blocks no good one. We measured twelve small open-weights monitors on payment approval under two pre-registered protocols. Without pre-registration, we also measured three closed frontier models (Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 4 Argon) and the open DeepSeek-V3.2. Every reliable fooling of a monitor into approving a fraud came through an evidence source and reached only that source's readers. Fooling it into blocking a correct payment depended on injection resistance, a monitor's refusal to follow instructions planted in its data. Small models and DeepSeek obeyed such notes. The three closed models ignored them in all but one case, and Opus also resisted persuasion tailored to it. On new data, a rule that counts sources instead of votes blocked 0.9% of correct payments, against 7.4% for the best counting rule, at equal safety. The pre-registered worst-case test failed. One attack left the approvers on a single source, so no rule over the twelve language-model monitors survives every measured attack. Adding a rule engine, which cannot be persuaded, restored the condition for a safe and live rule on the measured attacks. Diversify the inputs, harden the monitors, count sources, not votes.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The modeling of the behavior of agents in strategic environments and the prediction of the resulting outcomes has long been a challenging problem; this has been the focus of game theory. The introduction of AI agents as human-aids or as sole decision-makers expands the underlying question: Can we model behavior and predict outcomes of strategic games that involve a mix of AI agents and human players? As an initial answer, we propose Correlated Quantal Response Equilibrium (CQRE) that combines and generalizes classical solution concepts such as Quantal Response Equilibrium and Correlated Equilibrium. We answer questions of existence and propose a method for computing the CQRE that is a best fit to a given joint action distribution. We demonstrate the empirical effectiveness of CQRE predictions using a diverse collection of complex general-sum games, including high-rank and large-action two-player games, challenging multiplayer games, and a large-scale extension of the Selten--Chmura setting to AI--AI and human--AI play.

Language-model agents are increasingly asked to run experiments, yet benchmarks rarely measure whether those experiments improve the decisions they are meant to inform. We introduce CrashGym, a deterministic, replayable limit-order-book simulator in which an agent must choose between a deleveraging intervention and a liquidity backstop for a market about to suffer a shock-triggered crash. Before committing, the agent may query intervention experiments in a laboratory realization of the market. Its choice is then scored on an independently seeded target realization in which the simulator executes every feasible intervention, so regret relative to the best intervention is computed by directly simulating every alternative on the same target repeats, with no human or model-based judging. The simulator implements each amplification channel---persistent price impact, liquidity withdrawal, margin-driven liquidation, and an evolving strategy mix---as an explicit mechanism that can be switched on in stages. In a prospectively specified study on 24 newly sampled worlds, laboratory access reduces the mean regret of the one deployment with a complete record (Luna) from 8.878 to 3.785, a paired reduction of 5.092 utility units (nominal 95% world-bootstrap interval: 1.028--9.507), or 57.4% of the OBSERVE-ONLY mean. Prospective comparisons for two further deployments are incomplete; in a separate exploratory study, mean regret is lower with laboratory access for all four deployments evaluated. A laboratory whose strategy mix evolves endogenously yields no established advantage over one with a fixed mix. CrashGym thus measures the value of experimentation as avoided decision loss and lets simulator detail be judged by the decisions it supports.

An LLM multi-agent system (MAS) is only as good as the agents it chooses to trust: its accuracy and cost hinge on its topology, meaning which agents are included and how they communicate. A single task score, however, does not reveal which agents help or hinder performance. We propose Contrastive Attribution Topology Search (CATS), which searches for compact teams within a fixed supergraph of specialized agents. An LLM attributer compares execution traces across candidate topologies and assigns credit to individual agents. CATS uses these credits to update supergraph edges while progressively pruning weak edges and agents, yielding a small team for deployment. With small open-weight models and matched candidate evaluations, CATS improves mean accuracy on BigCodeBench by 5.3 percentage points over score-only heuristic search while using 54$\%$ fewer deployment tokens. On MBPP, CATS matches the strongest baselines with fewer tokens than the other searches. In a HotpotQA prompt-poisoning stress test, CATS excludes all adversarially prompted agents in all three runs, whereas random search retains some at comparable accuracy. Per-agent credit thus supports both team optimization and the pruning of potentially harmful agents.

As LLMs expand their language coverage, evaluating how well they understand and represent diverse cultures becomes increasingly important. However, many benchmarks remain English-centric, with limited cultural coverage and a focus on factual knowledge over its application in real-world cultural contexts. We propose CulturalRiddles, a benchmark of original, culturally grounded riddles created entirely by humans through a participatory community effort, spanning 62 cultures (45 countries, 51 languages). These riddles are deeply rooted in their respective cultures and require abductive and compositional reasoning, alongside detailed factual and social knowledge, language skills, and an understanding of culturally specific associations. We benchmark 28 LLM configurations using both automatic and large-scale human evaluation. Even frontier models achieve at most 22% accuracy in some communities. We publicly release all artifacts alongside an open contribution process to expand the benchmark's linguistic and cultural coverage.

BackgroundInformal sandstone workers are exposed to multiple occupational hazards, yet evidence on their combined multisystem health effects remains limited.ObjectiveTo examine associations of cumulative work duration, occupational factors, and health behaviors with musculoskeletal, respiratory, dermatologic, and auditory symptoms among informal sandstone workers.MethodsA cross-sectional study was conducted among 92 informal sandstone workers in Northeastern Thailand. Data were collected using structured interviews covering demographic, behavioral, occupational, and health characteristics. Cumulative work duration was calculated from years of employment, months worked per year, and daily working hours. Multivariable logistic regression was used to identify factors associated with system-specific symptoms.ResultsMusculoskeletal symptoms were the most prevalent (89.1%), followed by respiratory (60.9%), auditory (47.8%), and dermatologic symptoms (41.3%). High cumulative work duration was significantly associated with musculoskeletal symptoms (aOR = 6.21, 95% CI = 1.02-37.76). Male workers had lower odds of respiratory symptoms compared with female workers (aOR = 0.20, 95% CI = 0.06-0.68). Higher noise sensitivity scores were significantly associated with auditory symptoms (aOR = 3.65, 95% CI = 1.73-7.70).ConclusionsCumulative occupational workload, sex differences, and noise sensitivity were associated with multisystem health symptoms among informal sandstone workers. Integrated occupational health interventions are needed to reduce long-term health risks in informal quarry settings.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: With the advent of digital technologies and emerging cyber threats, cybersecurity has become an ever-relevant concern in today's digital world. This review will cover new technologies in the cyber security field, typical cyber-attacks, and how to defend against them. It covers artificial intelligence, machine learning, block chain, cloud security, zero trust architecture and advanced encryption. The focus is on discussing the most significant threats such as ransom ware, phishing, data breaches, and supply chain attacks as well as preventive and responsive security measures. The review also includes implementation issues, privacy issues, and future research directions. In conclusion, the adoption of advanced technologies, the implementation of effective policies, and the promotion of user awareness are all crucial elements in fortifying cybersecurity and creating secure and resilient digital environments.

Mid-training (MT) is a training phase in LLM training pipelines that continues pretraining (PT) on smaller datasets of higher value. Taking the PT and MT phases as a whole, training usually starts with only PT data and then transitions completely to MT data. In this work, we view this complete transition from PT to MT data as a special case of a broader class of data mixing schedules that specify how the proportions of PT and MT tokens in each batch change over training. Under fixed total training compute and MT token budgets, we ask: Is this complete transition to MT data optimal for minimizing final MT loss? We show that the answer depends on the learning rate (LR) schedule: one data schedule may outperform another under one LR schedule, but changing only the LR schedule can reverse the outcome. Specifically, when the LR decays throughout continued training, introducing MT data earlier and mixing it with PT data lowers the final MT loss compared with placing all MT data at the end of training, but this result is reversed if we use constant LR. We therefore study how to jointly choose when to introduce MT data and when to decay the LR through ablation studies, and find that it is better to decay the LR only after MT data enters training. Finally, we develop a theoretical model that explains why the optimal data schedule for a fixed MT token budget depends on the LR schedule.

Web-searching Large Language Models (LLMs) have changed how users seek online information: instead of sifting through ranked lists of links, users read synthesized answers. This shift creates a new LLM vulnerability: a data-void exploit. Disinformers publish their narratives in search spaces where relevant and reliable content is scarce, i.e. data voids, then rely on the LLM's web-search to retrieve and then use, cite, or list those pages in its responses to data-void seeking prompts. Unlike classical search, where users see ranking cues and competing results, LLMs can obscure when an answer relies on sparse, unverified, or adversarial sources. We study this threat by varying the user's prompt tone - skeptical, excited, or neutral - and LLM choice - ChatGPT, Gemini, or Sonar Pro - as well as three attacker controls. The attacker can use one of five known strategies to construct and fill a data void with their narrative, host their content at varying levels of visibility from well-established, indexed domains to less established ones, and include generative-optimization engine features thought to boost citing by web-searching LLMs. We find that data-void exploits can succeed with only a single attacker controlled page. Across all conditions, attacker-content appears in LLM responses 31% of the time. User controls offer limited protection: while skeptical prompts slightly reduce success and slightly increase flagging or warnings in LLM responses, we find no evidence of large effects of prompt tone or model choice on success rates, although smaller effects cannot be ruled out. Overall, our results establish data voids as a practical inference-time attack surface for manipulating web-searching LLMs through strategically placed web content and highlight the urgent need for defenses against such exploits.

Physical prediction, inference and control combine incomplete mechanistic models with limited observations. We argue that data–mechanism fusion should be designed around the target quantity or downstream decision.
